subsubtopic: GRANT PAYMENT CRITERIA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, one of the growing list of fiascos from the recent tabling of the federal budget is that which involves a $3,000 grant to home buyers. Because of a rather astounding and serious oversight on the part of the Minister of Finance and his officials, the grant will apply only to those buying homes with insured mortgages which, under the National Housing Act must be paid by the buyer before purchase. In light of the fact that many home buyers will not be able to qualify for insured mortgages through NHA-approved lending institutions, and those that do, in addition to facing bureaucratic application-form delays, could be pre-paying up to $1,200, almost half the amount of the grant, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Ellis):
That the finance minister take immediate steps to see that the mortgage insurance restrictions are removed from these grants, and that the red tape delaying the approval and awarding of these grants be eliminated at once.

The November 12 budget was supposed to alleviate some of that distress, but it did the very opposite. It hastened bankruptcies and multiplied unemployment. Then came strike three, the June budget, and it put the icing on the cake for the destruction of Canada. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Patterson):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of pressing and urgent necessity. Whereas 18,000 Canadian auto parts workers are on lay-off; whereas Canada is the only major industrial nation which has been unable or unwilling to force Japan into signing an auto and auto parts trade agreement; and whereas Japan is unwilling to arrive at a more equitable export policy with Canada with respect to automobile parts and units, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans):

subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR MONTREAL TRUCKING COMPANY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance, not

July 5, 1982
Oral Questions
necessarily because it is a week since his budget but because, in the presentation of that budget, the minister talked about the economic crisis affecting Canada and the need for restraint. What justification can the minister give and what leadership is shown by the government in considering a bail out of a trucking firm in Montreal with a loan guarantee to the tune of $30 to $50 million, when that will necessitate changes in the ITC regulations and may very well open the door for all service industries, not alone trucking firms, to seek such federal assistance?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: QUERY RESPECTING POSSIBLE GOVERNMENT SUPPORT FOR MONTREAL TRUCKING COMPANY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like to tell the hon. member that no decision has been reached to provide assistance in this particular case. I take it from his statement and the tone of his question that he would be opposed to any such assistance or relief in this particular case. I will certainly take account of his representation before any final decision is made.

I thank the minister for the consideration of listening to a representation, Madam Speaker, but 1 asked a question. 1 would be much more interested in knowing what the minister thought about these fundamental changes in the ITC regulations which will open the door for applications for bailing out guarantees to all service industries and not manufacturing industries as is the present policy. If the minister feels there is help available for Maislin industries then, in effect, will every other service industry or trucking industry be knocking at his door?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, 1 believe that every precedent established usually incites further applications for assistance. On that proposition I have absolutely no difference with the hon. member. The content of his question is still speculative, however, because we have not reached any decision. There has been a request for assistance, but no decision has been reached. When a decision is reached the hon. member will be able to put his questions with more knowledge, and certainly I will be able to answer them with more knowledge. subsubtopic: POSSIBLE INVOLVEMENT IN MILWAUKEE RAILROAD COMPANY AGREEMENT
speechtext:
1 have a supplementary question for the Minister of Transport, Madam Speaker. In view of the fact, and I think it is a fact, that one of the main reasons Maislin is in trouble is because of its U.S. operations and the fact that two thirds or more of its business is in the United States, can the Minister of Transport, who reports for the Canadian National Railways, please explain to
the House-and this would be another example of government leadership and responsibility-how in the world CN, a Crown corporation, could be involved in a three-year operating agreement with the Milwaukee Railroad Company which is now in receivership to the tune of $250 million, with the option, after that three-year agreement expires, of taking over the company and accepting its $250 million debt? At the same time, CN has reduced container service to Halifax, has become bogged down in the CAST operation of Montreal which is costing taxpayers money, and last summer used the deficit position of VIA Rail as a reason for the minister to cut service back by 20 per cent. What justification or rationalization is there for CN, a Crown corporation, to act in this way?

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE INVOLVEMENT IN MILWAUKEE RAILROAD COMPANY AGREEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the answer is terribly simple. As in the previous instance, that decision has not been made. What CN has with respect to the Milwaukee Railroad Company is an option to buy in three years' time. The purchase has not been made. My hon. friend, who is an expert in transportation, knows very well that CN is already in the United States with the Grand Trunk, for example, which makes an interesting contribution to the financial welfare of the company. There is a border between Canada and the U.S., but freight goes across that border and it is considered useful for CN to have these facilities in the United States.

subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-EFFECT OF WAGE REDUCTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Finance. Having spent the better part of the last four days travelling the country I want to ask the minister a question which has been frequently asked of me. We have interest rates at a level which people cannot afford. We have inflation at a level which people cannot pay to meet. We therefore have unemployment at a level which, I think, is an all-time high in the modern history of this country, and productivity is down to a level which I believe is an alltime low.
People have asked me, and therefore I ask the minister, how can reducing the wages of people who, previous to the introduction of the budget, could not afford to buy the products being manufactured in Canada, help to get the country back on its feet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: THE BUDGET-EFFECT OF WAGE REDUCTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the way he has formulated his question because he has seen the logical progression from high interest rates to high inflation to high unemployment. That is, in a sense, the logic I have been attempting to establish in the House of Commons.
I say to the hon. member that if we are to break what he has described as the source of our difficulty, namely, inflation, we will have to reduce our income demands. That is the logic of the budget statement. If all income demands-and I am putting the emphasis on all-were reduced to 6 per cent, then price increases would drop to 6 per cent. That would be the inevitable result, and we would then be well on the road to success in the battle against inflation to which he properly ascribes the high unemployment we have in the country at the present time.
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question of the Minister of Finance? The minister will recall, I am sure, that during the period 1975 to 1978 when there were wage controls in this country, prices did not go down. In fact inflation rose at a level far faster than wages rose. I ask the minister again if he can explain the following to me.
If unemployment and low productivity are related directly to high interest rates, as the minister has admitted, and if it is true that people who did not have sufficient money to buy products prior to the introduction of the budget will not have any more money as a result of the budget and, therefore, will be in no better position to buy products, why did the government not tackle the root cause?
Why did the government not take steps to bring down interest rates and thereby serve the purchasing power of the people of Canada and the manufacturing sector in a beneficial way? That would have allowed the manufacturing sector to get back on its feet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the government did take the only durable step that can be taken to reduce interest rates. We are attempting to break the inflation psychosis in the country by talking about a 6 per cent world of income demands. That is the only way to reduce inflation and the only way to reduce interest rates. The hon. member has that logic in his mind, and he ought to interrelate all these factors because he has all the logic in his head to do it.
Madam Speaker, this could well be a book written by Lewis Carroll.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF WAGE CONTROLS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, given that the shock troops in this battle for 6 per cent are the public service employees, may I ask the Minister of Finance why he thinks it appropriate, proper and morally defensible to act to remove from the bargaining table all matters relating to collective bargaining and to move unilaterally to reduce the wages of people who sat down in good faith and negotiated wage increases? Does the minister really believe that, in the Liberal tradition, this is a morally defensible thing to do?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF WAGE CONTROLS
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, I think it is morally defensible-

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF WAGE CONTROLS
speechtext:
In the Liberal tradition?

July 5, 1982
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: IMPACT OF WAGE CONTROLS
speechtext: -because it is in the national interest and it is absolutely imperative if we are to move out of this very serious critical economic situation that we face. At the present time in the country we have to take exceptional steps, and it is an exceptional step that will be recommended to Parliament by the President of the Treasury Board to reduce the income settlements of the Public Service to 6 per cent and then to 5 per cent. That is exceptional. 1 admit that to the hon. member. It is justified because of the exceptional circumstances that exist in this economy and in various economies in the world. subsubtopic: WAGE INCREASE DIRECTIVE COVERING MINISTERIAL STAFFS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. It follows upon a remark just made by the Minister of Finance that it was in the national interest to limit the wage increases of public servants. If it is in the national interest to limit increases to public servants to 6 per cent in one year and 5 per cent in the following year, how can it be in the national interest for the minister to have signed a directive on last June 17 to increase the salaries of his political staff and the political staff of ministers-his colleagues and the minister-by 10 per cent? speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 have explained on a number of occasions that contracts and pay periods which came up for renewal prior to budget night were treated in a just and equitable fashion. In fact if the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton takes the trouble to read Bill C-124-

Madam Speaker, why does the President of the Treasury Board not do the honourable thing? Rather than defending the indefensible

increases for political staff, the appointees of himself and his colleagues, why does he not do the honourable thing and roll them all back so that the exempt staff will stand in exactly the same position as public servants?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald J. Johnston (President of the Treasury Board):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the point 1 have been making to the hon. gentleman is that the exempt staff does stand in exactly the same position as the public service. He would have us say that because these members of exempt staff are appointed by individual ministers, somehow they should be made particular sacrificial lambs. 1 do not accept that position whatsoever. Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the President of the Treasury Board. The sacrificial lambs about whom he is so concerned never went through any collective bargaining process or never had any collective agreement. Second, would he table the salaries of his exempt staff and of that of his colleagues over the last year so that we can see what happened last March or April with respect to wage increase for those self-same people, at the same time that he is asking every Canadian, not only public servants, to restrain themselves to 6 per cent?

They do not collectively bargain, and they were given 11 per cent. Is he suggesting that they should be rolled back as well? What about the RCMP? They do not collectively bargain. Madam Speaker, I was every bit as proud of my staff as I presume the minister might be of his. The difference is that the exempt staff were the beneficiaries of a sleezy, underhanded directive days before the budget. That is what it was. subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF GUIDELINES TO INCOME OF FARMERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. Since interprovincial marketing boards were set up to give farmers the assurance that the selling price of their products would cover the cost of production, and since the new budget intends to limit these return to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent formula of the Minister of Finance, while not controlling the input costs of energy, interest rates and other items, will the minister inform the House how he can impose this income and wage control upon farmers, given that there is no authorization in the enabling legislation to allow the minister to set prices arbitrarily?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF GUIDELINES TO INCOME OF FARMERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, every one of the regulated products but one that are under federal jurisdiction were under the suggested 6 per cent, which is something of which a lot of people are not aware. In Ontario, when they signed the contracts for approximately 15 products this year, there was only one over a 5 per cent increase. Some were as low as a 3.2 per cent increase. In some instances perhaps the marketing boards are ahead of us in controlling what we call inflation. I think they have given leadership, maybe even to government, but certainly they have provided leadership for many other people in our society in that they have agreed to take those kinds of increases early in the year. Some of those contracts were signed in March and April of this year by producer groups.
The Minister of Finance has also suggested that, under special circumstances, if increased costs take place, for example, the merits of an application can be considered if it needs to go above 6 per cent. However, if those input costs come down I cannot see any regulated price commodity or cost-pricing formula-I cannot see any of them asking for more than 6 per cent if the rest of society goes along with what we are suggesting. In most instances marketing boards have given that kind of leadership. All matters under the jurisdiction of the federal Minister of Agriculture have practically stayed under those ranges, except the industrial milk products.

subsubtopic: APPLICATION OF GUIDELINES TO INCOME OF FARMERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the minister is skirting the question by ignoring the principles. It sounds to me that what we are talking about is subversion of marketing boards.

Madam Speaker, under what legislative authority will the minister proceed with respect to these prices since these are all federal-provincial agreements? Will the minister be seeking provincial approval before proceeding, or will he implement the peace, order and good government clause in the Constitution, as the government did under the AIB legislation?

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, again all the hon. member has to do is check the records which will show, for instance, that eggs were minus 4 per cent last year, not an increase, and other poultry products were lower than what we are suggesting even this year. Again, I do not know what the hon. member is talking about because we have no jurisdiction over some of the provincial marketing boards. Some of them are very strong, and they exist in every province across Canada. It would be up to the provinces to provide guidelines for them. We have been doing some checking and I should be able to release some figures, hopefully later today or tomorrow, to show exactly what some of them have done this year. I think it is to their credit that they have again provided that kind of leadership.
There is a misconception that many people have about marketing boards and the pricing formula that they follow. If input costs are down, they agree to take less. They do not agree to hold the status quo; they agree to go down in price. The only time that they increase prices to the consumers of Canada is if the input costs go up. They are very satisfied with that. Those farmers under programs such as those are the ones who are not going broke either. They run their own business, too.

The House resumed from Wednesday, June 30, 1982, consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government, and the amendment of Mr. Wilson (p. 18905).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when the debate was adjourned on Wednesday last to have a vote on the amendment to the amendment by the New Democratic Party, 1 was speaking about a number of things concerning the thrust of this budget that we have before us.
Over the weekend I was asked by a number of people, and I certainly have been asked in this House and so have others by members opposite, what we would do if we were the government, the kinds of measures that we would take in a budget to restore confidence in Canada. Madam Speaker, the first thing, of course, that we would do would be to eliminate the iniquitous provisions of the November 12 budget.
That budget was designed to destroy confidence, to destroy the willingness of people to risk their money and to destroy their desire to invest in Canada and create in Canada. That budget, with its horrendously complicated and vicious disallowance of loans, its vicious disallowance of capital cost on equipment and its anti-entrepreneurial stance in terms of taxation, is the kind of thing which has damaged Canada dramatically over the last eight months. We would have eliminated the provisions set forth on November 12. This minister did not do that, but that is the first thing we would have done.
Second, we would have seriously altered or suspended the operation of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. This country is desperately short of capital. The minister has said in answers in the House that we have a high savings rate, but I point out that while we may have a high savings rate in relation to the United States, our personal savings rate is less than half that which exists in Great Britain and less than one-third of that which exists in Japan. Second, our high savings rate is eroded by our high inflation rate. It is all very well to say that Canadians save up to 13 per cent of their disposable income, but when we have an inflation rate of 12 per cent, that
saving does not amount to very much. It certainly does not amount to enough to create the renewal required in our industries and to develop our many resources. We need foreign investment in this country. We need it in the worst way, and anything we have in our laws which discourages investment in Canada is anti-Canadian and anti-jobs, and that is the type of thing a government of which I would like to be a part would eliminate.
Next, we would seriously change the national energy policy. That policy, with its PIP grants and with arrangements made on the shores of Dow's Lake to determine where an oil company might drill and what kind of allowance will be given for exploration or development work, is anti-business. It is the kind of thing that is the clearest possible kind of demonstration of government's overriding control of the business community and business decisions. The very concept of the national energy policy's allowing the take-over by government of exploration advantages gained by those who explore under a 25 per cent back-in arrangement is anti-business because it represents expropriation without compensation. When we have those types of provisions in our law, what we in effect are saying is that private property has no sanctity here in Canada, and what we are saying to those who would invest in Canada is that they had better be careful because the government will back in on them or expropriate them without compensation.
Next, we would seriously attack the question of government spending. Government spending this year has increased from roughly $75 billion in the 1981-82 fiscal year to an estimated $90 billion or more in this fiscal year, an increase of well over $15 billion. There has to be some limit on this spending. What we would do is create an all-party committee of Parliament to go over government expenditures with a fine-tooth-comb to priorize government expenditures. I suppose there is nothing a government does that really is bad in terms of expenditures. At least the money is transferred to people or activities. However, there would be priorities. We would look at the priorities and try to eliminate as much spending as possible. We cannot go on forever trying to spend ourselves rich. What we must do is take a look at where we are spending money. Do we really need to increase the budget of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation? Do we really need to spend the money we are spending in foreign countries on foreign aid? Do we really need to spend the money we spend to promote exports, through the Export Development Corporation, to New York City, for example?
Are there a number of programs like CHIP, DIP and NIP which might be eliminated as being no longer absolutely required in this society at the present time? Can we not priorize government expenditures? I say we can, and I say a responsible House of Commons would have a committee which would go over expenditures working with the ministry to reduce government expenditures by 10 per cent. That would certainly eliminate a great many of the problems we have with
July 5, 1982

respect to the financial affairs of the country. If this country could reduce the amount it spends by 10 per cent, it presumably could reduce the amount it has to borrow by $9 billion. That would go a long way toward restoring confidence. While we continue to have a program of spend, spend, spend, we will not get anywhere. 1 say it is time we priorized our expenditures and seriously looked at expenditures to identify where we could eliminate or reduce government expenditures.
Next, we would make a direct attack on a whole series of alphabet soup programs this government has. We have alphabet soup programs in the fields of housing, enterprise development, foreign aid and culture. Indeed, we have alphabet soup programs in every field. We have agencies and groups. We have programs on programs. The book on ITC programs alone is nearly an inch think. We must look at these programs. What we are getting out of them is anyone's guess. One of the things a government interested in the enterprise system would do is quickly eliminate as many programs as possible and replace them with sensible tax incentives which would be broadly based and would enable the entrepreneur to use his imagination and not worry about a fancy application or detailed brief to some bureaucrat who must sit and read it and pass it on through his department until the program has lost its meaning and purpose.
One of the great problems with these programs is that they require applications and briefs. People are required to study them. Often the people studying them know very little, if anything, about the programs involved. They certainly do not know the detailed requirements which exist in the various parts of the country. Business people in the field know their problems and are prepared to attack them, but they cannot attack them sensibly or make our country grow sensibly if they are hamstrung and tied up by bureaucracy, by regulation and by controls. I say these are not necessary to make our country grow.
Next, we would have to do something about the serious shortage of capital in the country. Somewhere along the line we must do more to encourage saving. We must seriously examine the viability of the capital gains tax and the situation whereby we attempt to tax a second time around dividends of public corporations. Dividends are already taxed, or the income is already taxed, at the corporate level. When it is passed on to the shareholder, it is taxed again. It strikes me that there is no reason for this double taxation. The double taxation of dividends creates inordinate complications in the Income Tax Act and causes inordinate numbers of people to be working for Revenue Canada to analyse tax returns. It causes enormous problems for industry and business, and these duplications and costs should be eliminated if we are to obtain some productivity in the country.
Dealing with capital gains, I suggest to the government that this year would be an ideal time to eliminate the capital gains tax because this year is a year of capital losses. If the capital gains tax were removed, government revenue would probably increase.
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove

speechtext:
I thank the House for its indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and I will only take one minute more. I was speaking about the capital gains tax. This is a year when there are likely to be very significant capital losses. Under the Income Tax Act capital losses can be written off against income to the extent of $2,000. With the number of capital losses taking place now, I suggest to the minister that he might be better off to eliminate the capital gains tax completely and, therefore, the entitlement to write off losses. In fact, there are no gains to be made this year, or any that there are will be inflationary gains. More likely, there are deflationary losses, as our economy is in a tail-spin at the moment. Indeed, if anything it is on a run to bankruptcy. We must do a number of things to get this country back on the road to recovery. We must return confidence to the business community, to the farm community and to the home owner. Unless we do that immediately we will be in very bad shape.
In the few minutes allotted to me I have atempted to set out some programs that should be considered. They did not appear in the budget. The budget is remiss in almost every possible detail.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to express my complete support for the measures announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), particulary the initiatives which relate to my direct concern for housing.
This budget is designed to renew security and confidence, to foster partnership between governments and the private sector and individual Canadians and to achieve economic revival and recovery. It is designed to forge a national purpose and resolve to seek solutions to economic problems and to create jobs immediately. Nowhere are these themes more important than in housing. Housing is the cutting edge and it can lead the way to economic recovery.
To achieve this it is necessary to create a climate in which individual Canadians feel secure and confident in their housing choices. Home owners want to know they can cope with mortgage renewals, renters want to feel assured about the supply of rental accommodation and prospective first-time home buyers want a longer-term security before purchasing a home. This government, in past actions and through specific measures introduced by the Minister of Finance last week, has dealt with these issues. I will set them out one by one.
The Canada mortgage renewal plan will now provide grants. There will be no more interest deferral. Through the commitment to produce 30,000 rental units, the Canada rental supply

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
plan is reaffirmed. The $3,000 grant to buyers of new homes and first-time home purchasers provides immediate stimulus. Combined with the proposal set out in the white paper regarding mortgage funds at less than going rates, it provides a longer-term security framework. The additional 2,500 nonprofit and co-op housing units on top of the existing program for 25,000 social housing units will ensure that households on low and moderate income are not forgotten. Finally, the extension of the Canada home renovation plan enables more home owners to improve and repair their homes and thus to remain in their homes.
These actions demonstrate the government's concern for existing home owners, first-time home buyers, renters and for getting the housing industry and jobs in construction going. Canadians see housing as central to their social and financial security. These measures help restore that security. Confidence is needed if first-time home buyers are to purchase a home. This confidence is provided through the two measures I have discussed.

The measures taken by the government with respect to housing will give Canadians an opportunity to show a national resolve to stimulate the housing industry. To be successful, these measures require a definite commitment by, and the cooperation of, other levels of government, industry and our lending institutions. We must, all of us, work together with a sense of national commitment and purpose to get the housing industry back on its feet and pave the way for economic recovery. This is no time to point the accusing finger. This is a time for action and co-operation.

I am confident that if we all work together we will succeed in this mission, but it is no small job. Some housing analysts have been predicting housing starts will be in the order of
110,000	to 125,000 this year. I would like to see starts this year reach the level of last year, approximating need. This is an ambitious target in the present circumstances and my work, that of my provincial colleagues, the industry and all Canadians concerned will be difficult, but I believe that if we work together we can achieve real progress.
There are substantial rewards for the economy and for individual Canadians in achieving this task. Federal housing actions will create 180,000 jobs, most of them over the next year. These jobs will be in rental construction, the construction of single family dwellings and the renovation of existing housing. They will reduce substantially the high level of unemployment in the residential construction industry. Jobs will be created in the production of building materials and in the manufacture and distribution of appliances and other household furnishings. We know the spin-off effects these initiatives and support have on housing. These benefits will flow to all regions and parts of this country.
The federal government is committed to getting housing going and to restoring security and confidence. The government, through this and the previous budget, has allocated $750 million for housing initiatives in a period of some eight months. This is in addition to the government's ongoing
support for social housing, for rehabilitation under the residential rehabilitation assistance program, for home insulation, and for support of native housing. These are new funds allocated to housing. It is also important that hon. members and the public understand that these funds do not represent the replacement of private funds with federal funds. These funds provide incentives to Canadians. They represent the government working with Canadians to create an environment, a partnership, for economic recovery and for renewed security and confidence in the housing market.
This partnership between the government and individual Canadians means that this stimulus of $750 million in the last eight months will result in some $3.7 billion worth of new housing activity in the private sector.
I want to take a few moments now to review our programs specifically. I am particularly pleased with the decision to provide a cash grant of $3,000 to all purchasers of new homes and to first-time buyers of existing housing. I would like to remind hon. members that this assistance applies to all types of homes-single detached and semi-detached houses, triplexes, duplexes, row housing and condominiums. I have indicated that we recognize that under the National Flousing Act certain steps will have to be taken to get the grants flowing. The corporation has indicated that they are available as of the date of the budget. The grant is available for all new houses started before the end of 1982, including houses which are already built but not occupied. In the case of first-time buyers purchasing existing housing, the grant will be available to the end of this year. New houses must be purchased before the end of 1983 to qualify for the grant.
This time-frame, Mr. Speaker, is designed to encourage builders who are prepared to build housing on speculation. That is, to begin construction without a commitment from a buyer. We believe that this encouragement should have the private sector moving, because it is supported not only from the federal government but from a number of provinces who in the last few months have moved with similar or parallel programs.
To ensure that the buyer's continued interest in the property is secure and serious, a minimum downpayment of 10 per cent of the purchase price is required over and above the $3,000 grant. The grant, incidentally, is tax free. It is expected that this plan alone will encourage the production of medium-priced housing and, for that reason, there will be a price limit of $100,000 for all areas except metro Toronto, Edmonton, Calgary, greater Vancouver and Victoria, where the limit is $150,000 because of the difference in price ranges.
I noticed, Mr. Speaker, that on the weekend the real estate industry, particularly in metro Toronto, have taken advantage of the annoucement of these plans. Along with the $5,000 interest-free grant, it means, for example, that for condominiums offered for sale at anywhere from $35,000 to $50,000, the
July 5, 1982

$8,000 off is a considerable stimulus to that particular area of the market. The grant is a straight-forward arrangement. It will allow home buyers to take advantage of both the federal and provincial plans as 1 have noted.
The $3,000 grant has to be seen alongside the longer security aspect of housing which the Minister of Finance addressed on Monday last. Of course, I am referring to the white paper on the tax incentive plan. It is a document entitled "Inflation and the Taxation of Personal Investment Income" dated June, 1982, tabled with the budget material. It is a plan to give tax incentives and at the same time allow interest rates at 3 per cent to 6 per cent lower to be available to certain sectors in the economy. The preface to the document says:
They would also ease the cost of financing for new home buyers and small businesses, farmers and fishermen and increase the attractiveness of equity investments by individual Canadians.
The $3,000 grant is intended to be a bridge until the committee reports and the legislation is before the House and enacted. However, I would draw members' attention as well to the last sentence in the introduction by the minister:
-any legislative provision limiting qualifying property by an effective date will include purchases made after the date of issuance of this paper.
So that we see hand in hand an immediate stimulus in the context of a longer term security introduced by the provisions of those intended changes in the income tax structure.
As hon. members are aware, the government has already demonstrated its concern for renters and for the availability of rental accommodation through measures which will increase the production of rental accommodation by some 30,000 units. As you know, Mr. Speaker, one third-10,000-of those units are designed to be offered on a rent-geared-to-income basis to serve Canadians of quite modest income. 1 am very pleased to say that the $350 million program has been advertised and responded to by the industry, and the first project under that program is being announced today. It is in the Ottawa market where vacancy rates are quite low. The project cost is in excess of $15 million and comprises 343 housing units. It will have federal assistance of slightly more than $2.4 million, a per unit assistance of $7,250. Hon. members will note that the federal assistance results in over $15 million in construction activity. Thus, the $350 million will be used to generate affordable accommodation in the tight rental market. That program is on its way and I am particularly pleased to see that it is starting in concert with budget announcements in support of other housing measures.
1 am very pleased to say that the response has been encouraging despite, of course, the slow take-up time. I would have preferred the program to start earlier, but I am confident that the Canadian rental supply plan, with the $350 million allocated in November, taken in conjunction with the $400 million announced Monday last by the minister, introduces a major stimulus to the economy at this time.
The 30,000 units to be assisted under the plan, of course, are in addition to those the government supports presently under the co-operative and non-profit housing program which similarly encourages the construction or acquisition of housing
The Budget-Mr. Cosgrove
intended mainly for people with limited incomes. As you know, Mr. Speaker, another provision of the budget on Monday last was to increase that 25,000 units to 27,500, and I know that will be good news to a number of organizations right across the country who have expressed interest in sponsoring these socially useful housing projects.
One of the most popular of the government's recent initiatives in housing has been the Canada home renovation plan, which is helping Canadians to stay in their homes and renovate their homes. It provides forgivable loans up to $3,000 to encourage owners to invest in the renovation and improvement of their properties; that is, on the expenditure of twice as much of their own funds. That program was supplemented by an additional $30 million which means, Mr. Speaker, that Canadians will be using $60 million of their savings to support the stimulus of this program announced by the minister.
The public response to the plan has, of course, been overwhelming in many communities. CMHC reports that although the program has been in effect just two months, the total loans approved or in progress amount to almost $8 million of the original $30 million allocated. I welcome the minister's announcement. It is an effective program directed to need, and at the same time it is putting savings to work and getting Canadians working.
I think all hon. members will welcome the changes announced by the Minister of Finance regarding the Canada mortgage renewal plan which offered a combination of grants and interest deferral guarantees for home owners facing renewal at interest rates much higher than the rate on their original mortgage. Members from all parties have complained that Canadians did not respond because they did not want to get into further interest-deferral guarantees. The minister has set aside an additional $50 million so that this program will be changed with the passage of the legislation, but effective to the date of the announcement, so that any family renewing after Monday last and paying over 30 per cent of their income for principal, interest and taxes will now qualify for a grant to meet the difference up to $3,000 annually. This amount as well is tax free. I believe it is quite evident that many Canadians do not consider the interest deferral as attractive, as has been suggested. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that with this change we will see a renewed interest in the plan and applications will be taken up.
As I said at the outset, this budget is important for the range of initiatives taken in the housing area generally, where we have a shared responsibility with the provinces and municipalities. It increases the security of home owners faced with mortgage renewal, as I have just described, and concerned about losing their homes. It faces the difficulties of Canadians looking to rent, and I have announced the first plan under the rental supply program where $350 million is going to work responding to the 2,500 applications by builders right across this country. In my view, the budget provisions restore the confidence of first-time buyers both in the short and long term.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Clark
I have indicated that the $3,000 grant is intended to be an immediate stimulus, but in the context of the commitment of the government in the white paper it is to provide that framework of reduction in interest rates over the long haul, not only for home owners but, as the minister has indicated, for farmers, fishermen and small-business men. The budget provides confidence to the residential construction industry, to managers, to owners and to those people who invest and who are concerned about making starts, and stimulus is offered in cooperation, side by side, with some plans already announced in some provinces. In sum, it signals the government's concern and commitment to security for home owners and renters, to reasonable access to ownership and to the principle of the national government which is to work in co-operation with the provinces, municipalities, their agencies and with industry. We have as well considered representations from hundreds of Canadians received by members on both sides of the House over the past few months.
In summary, I want to indicate to hon. members that over the next few weeks I will be visiting my provincial counterparts and meeting with representatives of industry. We will be receiving briefs on the white paper, as the minister has indicated, on those areas of the tax incentive program that will bear on making housing more affordable and purchase more secure. I want to hear their comments on the white paper as well, so I can frame my responses to the minister. I want Canadians to know that this government gives high priority to getting the housing industry on its feet, to getting jobs going again and to boosting the housing industry in Canada. It will require not only these stimuli, not only this leadership and financial commitment of the national government, but the co-operation of all Canadians, my provincial counterparts, the provincial governments, the municipalities and industry.
This is the message of the budget. These are difficult times. Canadians are asked to respond together, and I am convinced that Canadians together can make it happen.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the House by commenting on the remarks of the minister responsible for housing. He has made predictions before about the effectiveness of his program in case after case after case. He has seen those predictions proved wrong by the reality with which Canadians have to deal. We hope he is right this time. We expect him to be as right this time as he was last time, and we trust that when it is proved he has failed one more time he will take his courage in his hands and resign along with his government.
