speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Most of us have been travelling the country for the last several months speaking to Canadians who are in acute difficulty who know, not as a matter of theory but as a matter of fact with which they have to live day after day after day, just how seriously their lives are undercut by the economic
policies being followed by this government. There had been some hope because of the persistent pressure mounted by this party in the House of Commons and elsewhere that we would get a new budget which would bring about a change in economic policy and some hope for Canadians. That was the hope. I could not help but remark the other day that the day after the budget was brought down on June 28 there was a chorus of criticism from across the country, informed criticism, people who knew that what was being proposed just would not work, and that criticism continued unabated. We have seen it in newspapers in this country and elsewhere. We have read it in the U.S. periodical Business Week which was quoted on the last sitting day by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). However, he neglected to quote from the most recent issue referring to this government's economic policies, which reports that the economic policies of this government have-
-brought Canada to the brink of economic disaster .. . The gross national product is shrinking, U.S. and Canadian investors are taking huge amounts of capital out of the country. Business is staggering under an unprecedented debt burden, and the Canadian dollar has fallen to an all-time low.
The article goes on as follows:
-many economists fear that companies' crippling debt load now eating up 66 per cent of corporate pre-tax cash flows will snuff out prospects for even a weak Canadian recovery this year, whether or not the U.S. economy revives.
The Wall Street Journal for June 30 has an editorial entitled succinctly "Poor Canada". It concludes:
The new budget is well designed to deepen Canada's stagflation.
We have read the same in Canadian newspapers. For instance:

Today, the Montreal newspaper La Presse printed an article by Mr. Yvan Guay, under the heading: "New Budget Puts Country into Recession."

And so it goes across the country. Every analyst and individual who has had the opportunity to consider the impact upon his or her life of this budget knows that it is a disaster waiting to happen to them. I see the Member of Parliament for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters) shaking his head. I would be pleased if either myself or members of my party could go to Thunder Bay to debate the impact of the budget upon the citizens of that coummunity. We would do a fatality count of the number of businesses that have been driven into bankruptcy in the Thunder Bay region. We would do a fatality count of the number of old age pensioners who will see their benefits reduced because this government is asking the elderly to pay the price of this government's incompetence. We would talk to people who have been forced out of work and to abandon their hopes and dreams in that community. We would then recommend to them that if they want a change, they had better send to the House of Commons a Member of Parliament who puts his people's interests ahead of his party line. That is the only way to get a change in this country.

July 5, 1982

[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we are faced today with a very serious crisis in our economy. The statistics are known to everyone. One million two hundred and forty-one thousand Canadians are out of work. The Canadian dollar is worth 77.56 cents in terms of the U.S. dollar. Interest rates are at 16.58 per cent and rising. Every day, 1,200 Canadians are losing their jobs. The desperation these figures are causing is absolutely heartbreaking. The fear of losing one's job, tension rising in families, marriage breakups, violence and suicide, all as a result of economic pressures. The cost in human terms is something we would rather not think about. The statistics are merciless, but although they cannot be denied, they can be manipulated and one gets used to them. But, Mr. Speaker, we do not get used to alcoholism, we do not get used to suicide or battered wives or family breakups. All these phenomena tend to increase when financial conditions get worse, and unfortunately, that is what is happening in Canada today. When discussing economic policies that are putting Canadians out of work, we must also consider the human cost. That is the point I am trying to make. We are talking about policies that are driving people to alcoholism, policies that are causing family breakups and bringing Canadians to suicide. That is what we must remember when we are discussing what is happening to this country. That is what we must not forget when we say we have a duty to our fellow citizens, because we here in the House are the only institution in Canada that is able to compel the government to act. The worst part of this recession is that the Government of Canada, a majority government at that, has no plan at all to get Canada out of this situation. And the unforgivable sin is that once again, this government is trying to trick Canadians instead of providing honest leadership.

I want to deal for a moment with the question of trickery. Trickery is the trademark of this budget and trickery is the trademark of this government. Consider just a few items, Mr. Speaker. First, a 6 per cent freeze is imposed on every public servant. But 11 days before the freeze a special class, people who work for Liberal ministers, received a 10 per cent raise authorized by the President of the Treasury Board. The man who holds back public servants makes a special deal for his friends who work for Liberal ministers. That is one piece of trickery.
The budget claims $750 million will be spent on job creation. The clear implication is that there will be $750 million of new spending, and that is false. At best there will be $267 million in new spending to create jobs. At worst it will be only $117 million in new moneys allocated this year to job creation. The practice was followed in 1979 of stating in the budget-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I think the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) might be interested in knowing that the Treasury Board
The Budget-Mr. Clark
decision to provide the 10 per cent wage guideline increase in fact was made on May 13.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What the Leader of the Opposition is interested in knowing and what the people of Canada are interested in knowing is that 11 days before the budget came down, a budget which the President of the Treasury Board knew would be imposing limitations upon public servants, the President of the Treasury Board decided to go ahead with a proposal which would give a raise to his friends who worked for Liberal ministers. What the country is interested in knowing is that the double standard is alive and well within government. There is one standard for most of the public service; there is another sweeter and fatter standard for those people who work for Liberal ministers of the Crown. That is the reality.
The minister grins about it. Instead of grinning, I should like to have him table in the House of Commons the order of June 17 and also the salary levels of those exempt staff before and after June 17, so that we will know exactly what is the situation. That would be a means of dealing with the accusation of trickery which 1 make here, the accusation that the government in this instance, as in so many other ways, is trying to trick the people of Canada into thinking that it is doing something which it is not doing.
Before the President of the Treasury Board rose, 1 was recalling to the House the fact that in the budget of 1979 introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) the practice was followed of stating in the budget the increase in unemployment insurance contributions. That was the practice in 1979. We knew the payments would go up so we told Canadians the truth. In this budget nothing is mentioned of the increase in unemployment insurance payments. The fact is that each employee in Canada will pay up to $142.50 per year more in unemployment insurance contributions; that is each working Canadian. In effect, that is a tax increase of another $142.50 for every working Canadian who contributes to unemployment insurance, but not a word of that was mentioned in the budget. In the honest budget of 1979 the increases were forecast. This budget which cannot be so characterized was silent on those increases.
Employers as a group-and it is not mentioned in the budget but it is there in the figures-will pay $1.2 billion more per year in their contributions to uenmployment insurance. That will drive some small businesses into bankruptcy; there is no question at all about that. It is a recipe for bankruptcy for some small businesses already on the ropes and ready to be knocked out of the ring. It is a secret tax of 52 per cent for employees and of 34 per cent for employers. The government admits that there will be increases but it refuses to say how much. This budget which is supposed to create confidence pretends that these increases are not there.
It might be fine for Liberal Members of Parliament to pretend that they are not there, but when Canadians pay $142.50 more next year for unemployment insurance benefits and when their employers risk going out of business because of this hidden tax increase which was smuggled into this tricky

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Clark
budget, they will know the high cost of having a government which cannot quite bring itself to be as truthful and as honest as the standards of this place and the country require.
I see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the Elouse. When the government was trying to justify having 1,200,000 senior citizens singled out to pay for the mistakes of the government, the Prime Minister said "6 per cent is what they will get; 6 per cent will be the CPI if we have co-operation". He knows that there will not be a reduction in CPI to 6 per cent. He knew it when he stood in his place; he knows it when he sits there now. He knows that the CPI will not be at 6 per cent and that the
1,200,000	senior citizens of the country will suffer from being singled out by the government.
And the deceit goes on. In housing there is a pretence of help with a one-time-only $3,000 grant. The average price of a Canadian home during the first quarter of 1982 was $75,578 across the country. Assuming an effective mortgage of $60,462, together with a builder buy-down of the mortgage to 17 per cent, the monthly payments on the house would equal $842. By applying a $3,000 one-time home buyer grant, the new home owner still faces payments on his home of $800 per month. The government will help buyers who can pay $800 per month. There are not very many of those in Canada, and there will not be very many Canadians who will be helped by this program.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about provincial grants?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
"What about provincial grants", I am asked by a Liberal Member of Parliament from Quebec who won and earned his way here by attacking Mr. Parizeau and Mr. Levesque. I am being asked why I do not come to the defence of Mr. Parizeau and Mr. Levesque here. The only thing I will say for them-

-at least the government of the province of Quebec, Mr. Parizeau and Premier Levesque are far more aware of the needs of their people than the Liberal federal government here, the government to which belong the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) and the Right Hon. Prime Minister.
As far as spending is concerned, this government claims that its expenditures-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What hypocrisy!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand), a former minister, talking about hypocrisy. At least he does not share in the hypocrisy of his Privy Council colleagues in government because he has been thrown out of the government. I would hope that if he sat there his standards would be sufficiently high that he would not associate himself as a minister with a government which has brought in a budget so full of deceit, so full of trickery and so empty of any hope of economic recovery.
[ Translation]
I was talking about spending and restraint policies. As far as spending is concerned, this government claims that its expenditures have not increased more than 17 per cent, while in the national accounts, the government's own figures indicate an increase of 20 per cent. During the election campaign, the Liberals promised to keep the rate of government spending below the growth rate of the GNP. That is another promise they have broken, and now they are spending twice as fast as they promised to do during the campaign. As far as small businesses are concerned, the budget proudly announced a $400 million program to, and I quote:
-reduce interest costs for small businesses.
However, the program is restricted to new investment. To date, 4,500 businesses have gone bankrupt in the first five months of 1982. How many businessmen, how many farmers or fishermen, assuming they would be interested, are in a position to make new investments?

This budget is designed to deceive. It pretends to be doing things it is not doing. That pretence destroys confidence. Nobody trusts a trickster, and a budget so full of tricks and so full of deceptions is bound to destroy confidence which is key to any recovery.
Apart from trickery, what is in the budget? There is one important initiative-the introduction of restraint on public sector salaries. That is a field in which the government has lagged behind several Canadian provinces. We are relieved that it is beginning to accept that government spending is a major cause of current economic problems. As usual, its proposal is unjust. It pretends that life is as hard for a senior deputy minister as it is for a clerk or secretary, and it applies the same restraint across the board, except of course for the staff of ministers. But it is a step in the right direction toward the government admitting that its own practices affect the economy.
Beyond that, beyond imposing restraint on public servants, old age pensioners and families with children, what is the direction of this budget? What is its purpose? What philosophy or attitude inspires it? What is the government trying to do with this budget? I suggest that it is trying to do two things. First, it is trying to buy time for perhaps yet another budget in the fall or, if we can believe the President of the Treasury Board in his remarks last Wednesday and the parliamentary secretaries from Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and Sudbury (Mr. Frith), to set the stage for wage and price controls in Canada. Apart from buying time, it is attempting to shift blame. The provinces have already been called in. No doubt big business will be called in and then the labour unions.
Anyone who has watched the confrontation tactics of this government for more than a decade will know that it is looking for someone to blame, someone to fight with, some scapegoat
July 5, 1982

to become its target and its excuse. The one area of unquestionable expertise in this government is setting up a straw man and attacking it. I would imagine that organized labour has been chosen for that role. The government wants to divert attention from its own failings and therefore it is looking for a fight with the unions. I hope that the leaders of organized labour will be wise enough not to be drawn into that trap.
Beyond buying time and shifting blame, what is the theme, the thrust, of this budget? Is it to restore confidence? With a $20 billion deficit and a hatful of tricks, is that the purpose? Is it to practise equity-that equity which was so much the siren song of the budget of last November; equity in a budget which increases taxes except for the rich; equity which singles out the elderly to pay for the government's mistakes; equity which imposes the same standard of restraint on a poor secretary in the public service as it does on a wealthy deputy minister? There is no equity in this budget.
Is its purpose to stimulate investment and thus create jobs? Obviously not when the government keeps in place the National Energy Program which has driven away billions of dollars of investment and when it offers small business, farmers, fishermen and the construction industry incentives which most of them cannot use.
The sad conclusion is that there is no purpose to this budget. There is no economic direction. This document is a short-term political response to an acute political problem. Since Liberal MPs just could not go home this summer with the government doing nothing, we have a camouflaged budget to make it appear as though the government is acting and then the subtle promise of another change in the fall.
We will see how comfortable Liberal MPs are this summer while defending a $20 billion deficit. We will see how comfortable they are defending a hidden 54 per cent increase in UIC contributions. We will see how comfortable they are this summer defending a $1.3 billion tax increase. We will see how comfortable they are defending a special plan to victimize old age pensioners. We will see how comfortable they are defending a special pay increase for the staff who work for Liberal ministers.
There is another remarkable feature of this budget, and that is the revelation that the June 28 budget did not belong to the Minister of Finance alone. It had a co-author, a co-conspirator so far unindicted. John Turner helped to write this budget. The Prime Minister smiles.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He likes that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: John Turner helped to write it and the Prime Minister leaked the fact that John Turner helped to write it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You should be ashamed of yourself.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East speaking again. I do not know if he is complaining that he was not consulted on the writing of the budget or if he is complaining about the fact that his friend,
The Budget-Mr. Clark
John Turner, is an unindicted co-conspirator in the preparation of this budget.
I must say that the Minister of Finance could not have chosen a more appropriate co-conspirator than the Hon. John Turner, because the spending policies that were begun by John Turner created much of the economic mess that we face today. It is entirely appropriate that we have a Turner-MacEachen budget because John Turner, along with the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), are the four horsemen of the economic apocalypse that we face in this country today.
An interesting tradition has been started. Years from now, in this tradition, when the roof of the Washington embassy leaks we will get Arthur Erickson to get the bucket. But I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance on persuading John Turner to carry the can for an economic crisis that he did so much to create.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those are John Crosbie's jokes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We just heard the Liberal party's jokes.
The reality is that a large number of Canada's economic problems were created right here in Canada and they can be solved right here at home in Canada. We can have economic recovery in Canada, but first we must put our own house in order. When the co-author of the budget, Mr. Turner, was minister of finance for four years, federal government spending rose by 108 per cent. That was in the 1970s. However, many of those spending programs became a continuing drain on governments. They created a situation where the cost of interest on public debt this year will equal $700 for every woman, every man and every child in this country and will equal $1,800 per taxpayer. That is the cost of interest on the public debt alone. We cannot afford that. We cannot afford the attitude expressed by the President of the Treasury Board last Wednesday at page 18965 of Hansard, when he said:
The essential attack on the federal deficit and on provincial deficits can only come when people contribute more out of their incomes to reducing them.
That comes from the minister charged with government restraint. He believes that the only way to cut the deficit is to force taxpayers to pay more. There, in a sentence, is what is wrong with this government. It expects others to act-the taxpayers, the Americans, the unions and the old age pensioners. That from the minister responsible for restraint, the minister who stopped the privatization program that would have cut government spending, the minister who stopped the introduction of sunset laws, the minister who stopped the legislation to control Crown corporations, if in fact he had any influence over legislation which comes under his jurisdiction. I quote again:
The essential attack on the federal deficit and on provincial deficits can only come when people contribute more out of their incomes to reducing them.
That is the quote. That is nonsense. The essential attack on the federal deficit must come from the Government of Canada

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Clark
cutting its spending, cutting its appetite and changing its attitude.
If the government does not want to start cutting expenditures, let Parliament start doing it. The Minister of Finance has set up a committee of outsiders to consider some of the measures he has announced, but measures he cannot produce, for this budget. Of course, that work should have been done by Parliament.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That will save a lot of money.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As one of my colleagues says, it will save a lot of money by bringing in these people, paying their per diem expenses and whatever else is involved. That will save a lot of money. That work should have been done by Parliament. Among other advantages, as pointed out by my colleague for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) during question period today, it would have allowed some women to take part in the process. The Minister of Finance discovered ten days after the budget that women constitute 52 per cent of the population of Canada. Before that, he had not deigned to allow one single woman to serve on this committee that he established. That eloquently indicates this government's position on the status of women.
In addition to recognizing the very existence of the majority of the Canadian population, a parliamentary committee would have acted with more authority than a group of advisers. However, that is behind us and it has been done. The minister preferred to go outside to bring in a group of men he could meet with in some dark room. Incidentally, I presume that women will be required to enter these committee meetings through the back door. The minister will probably not allow them to walk in through the front door as equals. He has indicated his chauvinism to such a degree that I imagine he will require them to go through the back door-once he finally finds a woman who is prepared to serve on the committee. However, the minister has made that decision and it is behind us. The minister went outside Parliament to do Parliament's work.
There is still a major job for Parliament to perform. It is a function that was proposed in this House some weeks ago by my colleague from Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). He proposed, and we propose again today, that the government establish immediately an all-party committee of Parliament to go through the government spending estimates again, not with an eye to the traditional approval, but to find areas where we can save on spending that does not need to be imposed upon Canadians, to identify programs we do not need, inefficiencies we cannot afford and expensive practices that are out of date.
That committee of Parliament, with the authority of Parliament could recommend where spending could be cut. It can prove to the government that restraint is a better answer to deficits than taxing the people. That can be done. It takes nothing more than a simple reference by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard). The committee could work all
summer. Certainly the members of our party would be prepared to work all summer. I would hope that the members of the New Democratic Party would do that, starting with what we learned in the examination of the estimates. Perhaps the NDP does not want to serve on a committee that works this summer. They had some difficulty showing up for a vote on their own motion the other night. Perhaps they would have difficulty showing up to undertake their responsibilities on that kind of committee.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take it that the contributions from the members of the NDP indicate they want to be dissociate from the rest of their party and indicate their willingness to work through the summer even if others of their colleagues do not. I will take it as that.
The point on this serious proposal is that a committee of this kind can work effectively and can work all summer. The need to do it was made abundantly clear in that abortive and frustrating exercise we all went through some two weeks ago when parliamentarians stood up in robot-like fashion and approved estimates that very few of us would want to take responsibility for in the public eye. That was a farce. We all know it was a farce. We know that Parliament and parliamentary control of public spending has become a farce. That is a reform for another time, something we hope will be reformed by the committee looking into it.
This is an urgent problem, a problem of trying to identify areas where we can save the taxpayers of Canada money right now and cut spending right now. Let us look at some of those things we know about. For example, we know that the Government of Canada spent $110,000 on a metric cooking lesson for Madam Benoit and Bruno Gerussi to help them carry out the propagandizing of metric in the country. Did we really need that $110,000 cooking lesson?
We know that each year the Government of Canada spends half a million dollars to buy briefcases that are given free to public servants, $500,000 so that public servants can have free briefcases. On the day that the post office became a Crown corporation, the Government of Canada, practising its usual restraint, spent $300,000 for free coffee, doughnuts and souvenir envelopes. That was to celebrate getting rid of the post office, or at least putting it into Crown corporation form.
We know there was a payment of between $365 million and $486 million too much for the purchase of Petrofina shares. We know about the JetStars that are used to carry ministers who will not talk to each other, one minister per JetStar to Winnipeg.
We know about the number of consultants employed by this government at extravagant cost. The federal government today has an information and advertising budget of $235 million. By the way, that is the largest advertising budget in Canada. More important, that $235 million which this government spends on propaganda is 17 times the total cost of government in the first year of confederation.
July 5, 1982

Those are just some of the areas where we know that savings could exist. That is just the tip of the iceberg. What we want to do is let the House of Commons do its job. The House of Commons should be allowed to go after not simply the tip but the whole iceberg. If we could cut seriously into that iceberg, we could save the taxpayers of this country millions, perhaps hundreds of millions, of dollars.
If we did that, we would not have to go to the old age pensioner and say to them that because the Prime Minister will not let Parliament do its work and cut savings, they will have to pay for it. They have to pay for giving Bruno Gerussi a cooking lesson in metric. We would not have to do that if Parliament was allowed to look into the spending carried out by this government, to find areas where we can cut back, so that instead of raising taxes for Canadians in order to reduce deficits, government spending could be cut on those programs on which the government has no business or no right to be spending money.
A profound difference in attitude separates the parties in this House. It is evident in the means that we choose to reduce the deficit. The government believes in taxing people more; we believe in cutting government spending, that is a symbol of a deeper difference about the role of government and the role of the state. Everybody accepts the responsibility of government to help the needy, the elderly and others. I should qualify that: everyone did accept that until the Liberal government singled out old age pensioners to pay for their mistakes.
The difference arises over the question of whether governments or people best encourage the growth and the freedom that have been characteristic of Canada. There has been with this government a steady movement toward control by the state. It is evident in the massive propaganda budgets which other free countries do not consider necessary to persuade their citizens but which has made the Government of Canada the largest propagandist in the land.
It is clear in the National Energy Program where state control has a higher priority than energy production and where the government has become a predator in the marketplace. It is evident in the attitude toward investment, frightening foreigners with F1RA and changing policies on IAACs, capital cost allowances and savings plans which would encourage individual Canadians to invest.
This government has adopted a deliberate anti-investment attitude. It used to pretend it was nationalist. The accurate word today is unemployment. Those policies have driven billions of dollars out of Canada and have cost thousands of Canadians jobs they would otherwise be working at.
Two weeks ago I gave the House several examples of the direct job loss in Canada because of measures in the November budget. I will not repeat all those figures. However, as an example, I want to remind the House that the provision on capital cost allowances alone has not been changed since the November budget. If we accept the estimate put forward by Walter Gordon's Canadian Institute for Economic Policy that $1 million in direct investment creates 40 to 50 jobs, and if we
The Budget-Mr. Clark
take the lower figure, the 40 jobs, then the government's decision to allow only one half of the capital cost allowance results in the loss of 44,000 jobs in Canada. Forty-four thousands jobs are lost because the government wants more more money and leaves less money for Canadians to be put to work. Those 44,000 Canadians could be working and paying taxes. They want to work. Instead, because of Liberal government policies they are forced to be out of work and to collect unemployment insurance. That is an economic waste. It is a tragic human waste. We cannot stand more of it in this country.
Those are only some of the costs. The anti-investment, antijob attitude of the Liberal policy also drives up interest rates. The National Energy Program is causing money to flood out of this country. Interest rates are used to bring that money back. If we had a pro-investment attitude in Canada, interest rates would be three or four points lower than they are today.
Projects that might be started in Canada are held back because the government's attitude creates a cloud of uncertainty. That affects large investors. It also affects individuals who have to make decisions such as buying a house, buying a car or starting a small enterprise. This country was built on taking risks, but no one takes risks in this atmosphere. It is interesting to note that when the uncertainty clears a little bit, Canadians will spend some of the money they have been saving. Canadians will buy.
I ask the House to consider what began as a fiasco. Consider the question of the Iraqi cars. Last month those cars went on sale at $6,500 each with a two or three-year guarantee. I spoke to a dealer in one city in Ontario who was allotted 200 cars for his dealership and 130 for his dealership in another city. Those 330 cars were sold out within 48 hours. What is interesting is that 95 per cent of the buyers paid in cash. That was the case with virtually every other dealer in the country. There were
12,000	cars put up in this country where risks are not taken because of this government. But in a circumstance where there is a good deal and a guarantee of two or three years, 12,000 Canadians went out and bought them in 48 hours-and 95 per cent of them paid cash. That means that they have cash waiting there to invest. They have cash waiting to put into the creation of jobs, but they will not put it into the creation of jobs in this country because they are afraid of what this government will do. That is an inexcusable situation in a country like ours.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The message from all of this is clear. Canadians are saving furiously. Why are they saving furiously? Because they have not got the foggiest idea what is going to happen to them in the future. There is nothing above them but a great black cloud of uncertainty about what this government is going to do next to gouge them. What old age pensioner would have thought, on the night of June 27, that he or she was going to be singled out for a special attack by the Liberal government? No

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Clark
one knows who is going to be attacked next by this government. Consequently, people who have money are holding it; they are not letting it go to work for Canada. They are not letting it go to work for themselves. This government's attitude is driving Canadians away from the creation of the kind of wealth and job opportunities that are not only key to this country but are at the core of our growth and our development as a nation.
Canadians do not know whether they are going to keep their jobs or lose them. As they look down the street, almost every Canadian has a neighbour somewhere on his or her street who has lost a job. When you are in that situation, you worry whether you are going to be next. Those people do not know whether they will have to renew their mortgages at much higher rates.
Even with all those uncertainties, there are two circumstances under which Canadians will spend some of their savings. The first is an exceptionally good deal, as whith the Iraqi cars. The second is an improved economic outlook and some degree of certainty that removes their fears for their future personal security.
There will not be many Iraqi deals. We cannot count on them to stimulate the economy

although it is interesting that in this regard, by refusing a contract, the government of Iraq has probably done more to stimulate investment in this country than the Government of Canada has. We cannot count on that. What we have to do is remove the uncertainty that hangs like a pall over every individual Canadian with money to invest. As long as Canadians who arc working and have money continue to save at such a high rate, the demand that results from consumer spending and risk investment will be soft. We will not be getting the jobs, we will not be getting the growth, we will not be getting the recovery we require.
The only answer is a set of economic policies that will restore confidence in the future of the Canadian economy. Those will cause increased spending by individuals, by companies, and that spending in turn will stimulate demand and increase production. But you do not create confidence with $20 billion deficits. You do not create confidence with a commitment to the continuation of the National Energy Program. You do not create confidence with a budget that tries to trick people.
What this country needs, and what it needed on June 28. is a new budget. What the country also needs is a new minister. What the country needs most of all, as suggested in the amendment, is a new government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What a new government should do in quick, summary form is, first, to follow policies that encourage investment positively, investment by Canadians and by others, to make this again a country where people can count on their investment being respected, where they can count on being free from knocks on the door in the middle of the night, or expropriation by legislation-such as the Prime Minister is smiling about now and such as he has introduced. We need to establish that climate of confidence to encourage positively investment in Canada by Canadians and others.
Second, we have to develop encouragement by incentives which cause individuals to make their own decisions to invest. There is a choice for government. Two mechanisms are open to them. They can use grants which give control to the government; or they can use incentives which leaves liberty to individuals. We have had too much control by governments, too much of grants which are susceptible to that kind of control. We need to move again to a system that creates the incentives that will allow individual Canadians and others to make the decisions that will cause the nation to grow.
Third, when a government introduces new economic policies, it has to indicate very clearly that those policies are going to be there to stay. We cannot have a situation such as we had with the June 28 budget, where everything is under review; where they propose programs that might or might not be introduced. We have to have some degree of constancy, some degree of certainty, in the programs that are introduced by government.
Fourth, there has to be a restoration of the movement towards serious restraint in government that was a feature of the government of 1979 and 1980. There has to be a return, for example, to sunset laws that will require agencies when they have been established to prove their continued viability, their continued need to exist.
There needs to be some opportunity for committees in this House of Commons to hold to account groups like the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, groups like the Export Development Corporation, others who function now, spending or committing millions of dollars of Canadian money without any effective control-no control by their board, no control by ministers, no control by the House of Commons, simply a licence to spend. That kind of thing cannot be allowed to continue. That kind of thing needs to be changed, and it can be changed in a way that is entirely consistent with our parliamentary traditions and that protects the nature of those agencies.
Again, we have to have a new government that emphasizes productive expenditures by government in growth fields, in fields like research and development. I believe the minister responsible for science and technology is due to speak next. I will be interested in his explaining why the government has reduced the target of the gross national product from the target established in 1979-80 to a much lower target. We should be investing much more now in productive fields like research and development, science and technology, which create jobs and give us a cutting edge for the future.
We should also be investing more money in long-term job creation, to allow men and women, particularly younger, but not exclusively younger, men and women, who want to play a full role in the modern work force, the opportunity to play that kind of role. We should also be creating a system of incentives to encourage individuals to invest in this country.
A new government that is trying to recreate confidence in the country should replace the National Energy Program with a program that will encourage Canadian companies to find oil and gas in this country, not simply to aggrandize, to expand,
July 5, 1982

the role of the state without increasing our capacity to become self-sufficient in energy.
Fundamentally, what we need of a new government in Canada is a recognition that we can solve in Canada economic problems that are caused in Canada. We need a government that will encourage individual initiative and that sense of adventure and risk that have always been key to this country.
Finally, we need a government that will establish an atmosphere of confidence and of trust so that Canada will regain the reputation we once enjoyed as a place where investment was respected, where the word of the government was respected, where the desire to work and to create was not only respected but encouraged.
Those things need to happen if we are going to pull this country out of the economic decline in which we are sliding. This government cannot do it. The only way it can be done is for the amendment before the House to be carried, for this government to lose the vote of confidence. The Prime Minister is in the House. If the Prime Minister is so confident about his economic policy, his and John Turner's, he should take those economic policies to the country. If he believes that his policies are correct, let him ask the people who are affected by them. Let him call a general election.
I hope that if he is not willing to do that, there will be at least enough of his former supporters in the backbenches who will recognize that the country is more important than their party, who will recognize that this nation needs recovery which it cannot get from this government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, never since the Great Depression have the people of this nation required a deeper, more profound and imaginative change in economic policy than precisely at this moment in our history. At the same time, never have I listened to a speech which was so systematic in its criticism of a government but which rested, in terms of its own fundamental analysis, on the same set of assumptions as those of the government party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with that in a minute.
1 do not want at this point to repeat a number of the truly alarming statistics about unemployment levels, about inflation levels and about people who are losing their homes. I do not want to repeat the pessimistic analysis provided by the OECD and the gloomy figures on the current level of the Canadian dollar. I will not repeat them. I will not do so because they are pretty well known. Day after day in the newspapers of Canada and day after day in all forms of news media the people of our nation are confronted with these figures. I will not repeat them, but that is not because they are not important. It is a basic task of politicians and political parties to see the relationships between these figures and to look for certain patterns in terms of analysis and in terms of a prescription for what might be done about them.
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
I want to say today that it is very important for us not to become jaded by these figures and not to become overwhelmed by the data because we see them day after day. That is a very easy tendency, and it is also very easy for us as politicians to become cynical, to say that because we see this unpleasant factual information hour after hour and day after day, there really is nothing that can be done and to use the data in a cynical fashion. Once there is the slightest impulse among politicians to see these figures in a cynical fashion, we should resign as Members of Parliament, because if there is one group of people in a free society which has the moral obligation not to become cynical, it is the people who are elected to do the government business of the nation.
Part of what stops me from being cynical, I suppose, in the face of this morass of figures is our actual confrontation with people who are the real entities behind the statistics. I have heard unemployment figures in the last couple of days. Two weekends ago I met a middle-aged man in the constituency of the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). That middle-aged man has two children and his wife is pregnant with a third. He was profoundly unhappy. For the first time in his life he was unemployed and saw his unemployment insurance benefits running out. He did not know what he was going to do. I thought he was on the verge of tears when he spoke to me, one man to another. When I hear these figures, I think also of other parts of Canada.

The unemployed fail to understand why a wealthy province like theirs is now experiencing such a high rate of unemployment, to the extent that in the manufacturing sector alone,
50,000	jobs have been lost since September. Unemployed Quebecers fail to understand why this is happening in a province as wealthy as Quebec.

In relation to mortgage problems, I am reminded of two weeks ago today when I met with people in my own constituency who had problems. Among them was a woman in her fifties who had two children and a mother to support. This woman was employed, and at a good salary for a working person in Canada. Her husband was killed a year ago and she came to see me about her home. For her it was not a residence, it was not a house, it was a home, and she described it in that way. She was concerned because her mortgage was coming up for renewal this month and she was to pay $200 more. To use her words, she was going to lose her home and her kids' home unless something was done, and done soon.
The point is that all these problems must always be remembered in terms of the personalities involved. They must be remembered in terms of the men, women and children out there in our country from one coast to the other who are experiencing real difficulty. These are men and women of emotion and frustration and, increasingly I regret to say, men and women who are experiencing fear about the future for themselves and particularly their children in this land of ours.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
It is the context in 1982-not 1932-that we must assess the budget presented by the government.
I think there are three useful ways of looking at a budget. The first is to look at it in terms of its technical information, its own analysis of the economy, its own forecast for growth, its own predictions about inflation and also in terms of the technical prescriptions prescribed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to deal with economic problems in the coming year.
Second, the budget should be looked at in terms of fairness or equity toward the problems faced by the people of Canada at this point in our history. Does the budget address those problems not only with some technical competence but also, in terms of its urgings upon the people of Canada, with a sense of fairness about the distribution of burdens in dealing with our problems?
The third way of looking at the budget is a little deeper and different from the first two, as important as they are. What does the budget, a financial statement, say about the government's understanding of the Canadian economy and, beyond that, Canadian society at a particular point? A budget does that either directly and explicitly or indirectly. It is very important that we understand budgets in that context. Where does the government want us to go? That is the relevant question one should pose at some time in looking at a budget. What does it want us as a people to do?
I want to discuss each of these points. First, in terms of the technical detail, what are the relevant facts in the budget as I, my colleagues and our financial critic who spoke so well the other day see them? First, we see that taxes are going up by $1.3 billion for all Canadians. We see that pensions and family allowances will be going down, in their net effect, by some $360 million. We see particularly that wages in the public sector will be held at 6 per cent in the coming year and 5 per cent after that in terms of increases. If we include the armed services in that, as we should, that will take some $1 billion out of the economy.
Then, as the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) mentioned in his speech this afternoon, in terms of budgetary analysis at this time we must include changes in the unemployment insurance fund. We note that every employed Canadian will pay somewhere in the neighbourhood of $140 more in the coming year as a result of drain on the unemployment insurance fund.
If we add all these together-taxes going up, pensions and family allowances going down, wage controls in the public sector and increased premiums for unemployment insurance- what we will see in the coming year, in the face of the most serious unemployment level in this land in the past 50 years, is the taking out of the economy of some $4 billion.
What is the result now? What are the implications of this program, first, for the so-called crusade that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) spoke about the other day and about which the Minister of Finance talked as well when he presented the budget? They spoke about the "crusade"
against inflation. Was there anything in the budget that dealt with the most serious price increases that have affected the Canadian economy in the past 12 months and will continue to affect it, namely, interest rates and energy costs? There was not a thing, Mr. Speaker. Those prices are not going to be controlled and they are not going to be changed. Nothing is to be done about general interest rate levels, which are so pernicious in their effect on the economy. Indeed, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated in the House the other day, no attempt will be made to renegotiate or delay the energy price increase of another 30 per cent in the coming year. No attempt is to be made at this particularly difficult time in our history to talk in a co-operative and serious way with the producing provinces to see if we can delay the impact of these monumental price increases which are yet to come in the energy field. Nothing was done seriously about prices in the budget.
Where is this crusade-to use the wonderful word of the President of the Treasury Board-to have its focus? We know it is going to be on wages. 1 think it is relevant to ask whether an approach on wages in the past, in terms of government policy, had any impact. From 1975 to 1978, when the government was at least claiming to be dealing with prices, what was the result? The A1B program at that time was described as being aimed at bringing down the level of inflation by 4 per cent by the third year. Instead of going down by 4 per cent, the rate of inflation actually went up by 1.5 per cent to 9 per cent. It was successful in holding down the wages of ordinary men and women, however. The Conference Board estimated that there was a drop of some 8 per cent in wages compared to what there would have been had the controls program brought in by the Prime Minister at that time not been imposed.
Surely it is a relevant question from a technical point of view for anyone who wants to understand inflation, from the humane point of view or from the point of view of concern for moral justice, to ask why with this past record, the government is bringing in a program that singles out public sector employees for such controls.
The answer to that question was revealed in a secret cabinet document to which I had access last year and which I released to the public of Canada. In that document there was an analysis of the causes of inflation and of what the government might consider as options. The document said that the "main advantage"-and those are the words used in the document- is that the government would be seen to be doing something. Not that the program would be effective, or not that inflation would be brought into line-because they knew from the experience of 1975 to 1978 that it did not have an effect on prices-but the single merit underlined in that document was that such a program would demonstrate to the people of Canada that the government was at least doing something.
I think that when you make victims of men and women, in this case in the public sector, simply to save political face, then
July 5, 1982

the only way to describe such action is to say that it is despicable, and I say that without hesitation, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Elear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The reality is that in Canada in 1982 we do not have wage-generated inflation. The reality is that the Minister of Finance admitted that himself some months ago. The reality is that the so-called crusade and symbolic leadership is just the opposite of leadership; it is a cynical public relations exercise of the worst kind-the kind that first makes scapegoats of employees in the public sector and then sets up as future scapegoats every working person in this country. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, it is despicable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This unfairness is compounded when you consider that not only are wages to be controlled, but that with this partial deindexing of family allowances and pensions, the same ordinary people are going to be hit twice.
It should be noted, however, that there is an interesting hypocrisy to be found in the budget. Investors will now be better off because the Liberals accepted a Tory ide^t. While the Liberals are busy taking away indexation provisions from the average taxpayer, they are simultaneously introducing new indexation benefits for investors that the Conservative Party, as its finance critic said some time ago, first advocated.
I think that is a perfect example of what has come to be known as supply side economics, which operates on the interesting moral precept, that in order to get the rich to work harder you have to give them more money, and in order to get the average Canadian to work harder you have to give him less money. Anyone who believes that would believe anything.
How does this budget stand up, Mr. Speaker? Over all, in terms of fairness and equity it is clear that it fails considerably, certainly from the point of view of distribution of burden. Obviously, also, it will not bring down the rate of inflation to 6 per cent. I repeat, in the experience from 1975 to 1978 at least there was some alleged attempt, in a comprehensive package, to control prices as well as wages, but in this budget there is not the slightest suggestion that determined action will be taken against any other group than wage earners. I say that there is not an intelligent person in the House of Commons or a member of the cabinet-and members of the cabinet are not stupid; they may do stupid things but they are not stupid, not even the Minister of Finance who is sitting opposite at the moment-who seriously believes that inflation will be brought down to 6 per cent by the end of this year. They claim to believe it, but it is a bogus argument.
I should like to deal with a different matter and that is one which the President of the Treasury Board dealt with in his speech at considerable length and which the Minister of Finance has dealt with time and time again. It is our so-called international position.
Are we as a nation going to remain internationally competitive? The great justification for this wage control approach that is at the core of this budget is that it is going to make us
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent
internationally competitive; that it is required for that reason. In this, Canadian workers are once again being made the scapegoat for the failures of Canadian governments and, to put it bluntly, for the major sectors of Canadian industry. In fact, perhaps the most serious failure of this budget is that it does not face directly the very real problems of Canadian industry in the tough, competitive international world.
What the budget does in this regard is to place the completely wrong emphasis on wages and salaries. That is an extremely serious mistake because it focuses on the wrong target and ignores what ought to be stressed. In this context 1 urge the minister, who is sitting opposite this afternoon looking rather bemused in some kind of metaphysical mist, to read an article written by two interesting people, R. H. Hayes and W. J. Abernathy. The minister will be interested to note that it does not appear in a socialist publication or a progressive liberal publication, if that is not a contradition in terms these days. This article, Mr. Speaker, appeared very recently in the Harvard Business Review and is called "Managing our way to economic decline". I urge the Minister of Finance, the Tory finance critic and his leader to read that article because it makes an extremely serious argument, one that I understand is now at last being taken up in American business circles. Perhaps their Canadian counterparts will soon take it up and hopefully the government will pay some attention to it. It diagnoses the problems of North American industry, but are they due to wage increases, government regulations, all the cliches I have just heard from the Leader of the Opposition and repeated in a different form by the minister himself in recent weeks? No. What it says-and I say it applies with much more relevance to the Canadian economy than to the American economy-is that the central failure of North American business is that for many years now it has wrongly put the emphasis on short-run profits and has insisted, as a fundamental part of its operation, on short-run cost reduction. That is to say, keeping wages down instead of emphasizing, as the authors point out, the necessity of looking at the long term, the necessity of doing more research and development and putting emphasis on quality products. Most specifically and relevantly to this budget is the authors' argument that northern European labour costs are now the highest in the world and this has not hindered them from becoming extremely competitive in the modern international atmosphere. The key, positive point that they make is that the Europeans and Japanese plan for the long run, put much greater emphasis on research and development, and, contrary to the methodology of the Conservative Party on my right and the practice of the Liberals across the way, both Japan and northern Europe have much more intervention in their economies by government than we have here in Canada or in the U.S.
1 want to say in that context, Mr. Speaker-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
More government intervention!

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Broadbent

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Exactly. 1 want to say in that context that I listened to the Leader of the Opposition making his criticism of that hopeless gang across the way for the cruelty they have inflicted on the people of Canada, but I must say that he trotted out every old Conservative cliche that I have heard in this House for the past 14 years. The single important virtue of Ronald Reagan, Mr. Speaker, is that he at least was an honest Conservative.
We heard from the Leader of the Opposition the cliche about the need for less planning and government involvement. We heard him say that we need to have less of what he called control by government. In particular, there had to be less government spending. Well, I say to him that his own members have been demanding more government spending on pensions, more government intervention in housing, in fisheries and other areas, and I repeat: at least Ronald Reagan is honest. He wanted a cutback in government involvement and activity, but he laid it on the line about what programs he was prepared to cut. That honesty I can respect even though I disagree with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I want to make about the serious problems of Canadian industry which should have been but were not addressed in this budget is that this government had made not only an unfair policy decision as it affects wage earners in this country, but a tremendously erroneous judgment about what is really at the heart of the malaise in Canadian industry. This budget completely lacks an industrial or manufacturing strategy, one that puts its emphasis where it ought to be, namely on the crucial need for Canadian governments and businesses to co-operate in more planning, not less. That is the real need of the Canadian economy and we should have had it firmly expressed in this budget.
Having said that, I also want to say something about the short-run effect of taking so much money out of the Canadian economy. I mentioned earlier that the net effect of tax increases, pension and family allowance reductions, control of wages in the public sector and the coming increases in unemployment insurance premiums is that it is going to take over $4 billion out of the economy. This, precisely at a time when stimulus is needed. It will not mean more jobs, it will mean less jobs. Instead of learning from the errors of the 1930s, the Liberals are repeating them. Instead of stimulating the economy this summer by a tax cut, we are mindlessly increasing taxes. Instead of improving upon the recession by creating more jobs, the Liberals are going to deepen it. In that context, Mr. Speaker, instead of clinging to office this government should resign.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we desperately need more jobs now for the men and women who would rather be working, paying taxes, and producing goods and services than collecting
unemployment insurance or welfare. We in the New Democratic Party say that now is the time to stimulate the economy, not shackle it. Now is the time to provide hope and confidence, not by false statements, silly cliches or contradictory policies of the kind we are getting from the Conservatives, but by describing the situation honestly and distributing the burden fairly.
We say in the immediate sense that what we need is a lowering of taxes now. We need a further expansion of housing programs. We do need and could have lower interest rates if the Minister of Finance would exercise his authority and tel! Governor Bouey to bring them down. We do need a serious attempt by the Prime Minister or the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) to negotiate with the producing provinces a delay of the increase in the price of oil which came on the first of this month and the consequent and equivalent price increase of natural gas which will come-
