subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 will not abuse the generosity of the members of the House by taking much more time. I have said we need more stimulus now, and I do not hesitate to say that at this particular point in our history. We should learn from the 1930s instead of repeating those errors. That is what we should be doing.
Having made three or four short-run proposals, I want to conclude by saying that the most damning criticism of this government at this point in our history, when other nations are taking their industrial development with greater seriousness and paying it greater attention, is that this government, this collection of individuals who call themselves a government, is totally indifferent to the need for planning a modern industrial nation.
What the New Democratic Party says, with more emphasis on this point than on any other, is that this was the time for us to have levelled with the people of Canada; that this was the time for the trade unions and the business community to have been called in. We ought to have said: "Yes, we will expect something of you. We will expect equivalent sacrifice, if you like, but in return we will give you a commitment over the next two, three, four or five years-because putting our house in order is not going to be done overnight-to rid ourselves of this old notion of continuing to be some kind of resource hinterland for the rest of the world, that instead with more government planning, not less, with co-operation of governments, the private sector and the trade union movement we will at long last do some serious planning and create in this country a manufacturing nation of the first order."
That can be done, Mr. Speaker. It ought to be done. The first step to be taken to bring it about is to get rid of the Liberal Party and the Liberal government. The next step is to elect the NDP.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member accept a question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member in his remarks said on several occasions that the government through its budget is taking considerable sums of money out of the economy. I believe he said that on the night of the budget as well. Could the hon. member explain to the House how he calculates that the government is taking considerable sums of money out of the economy? As I read the budget, every cent that is saved by putting limits on salaries, and so on, is going back into the economy in the form of job creation, housing and so on. As I read the budget, every cent that is saved in one place is going directly back into the economy in other places. Could the hon. member explain how he calculates that money is being taken out of the economy as if it were to reduce the deficit, which is not the case?
The Budget-Mr. Roberts

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I respect the hon. member, but I would also respectfully say in this context that he really has become a Liberal backbencher and been taken in by the old shell game of the cabinet. I would be glad to explain in detail to the hon. member, but I do not want to make another speech at this point the way as I did on budget night. What he says in fact is simply not the case.

speakeroldname: Hon. John Roberts (Minister of the Environment and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the budget which was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is realistic, responsible and tough.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is nothing for R and D.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman says there is nothing for R and D. That clearly indicates how little he has studied the budget. If he waits in the House, I will reply to that point a little later in my speech.
This budget is realistic because it concentrates action on those areas where the federal government's action can have the most impact on our economic situation. It is not an abdication but an acceptance of responsibility, to say that Canadian policy changes in themselves cannot change, alter or correct all of the world's economic problems. Canada as a major trading nation obviously is going to continue to receive the impact within our economy of economic events that take place outside. However, there are things that we can do to respond to Canada's economic problems, and those things this budget does do. It concentrates particularly-and there are clear indications that this is important-on counteracting those factors which lead to cost-push inflation, that is the increasing wage rates in the economy. This is one area where the position taken by the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and that of the government differ. The NDP does not appear to believe that wage rate increases taking place in the Canadian economy, particularly in comparison with that of our major competitor, the United States, are not a factor in the inflationary struggle that we face. Quite clearly, we on this side of the House believe that they are. The government has acted within its powers to respond to those wage rate pressures by bringing those wages in the public service under a capping control.
At a time when wage settlements in Canada are outpacing those in the United States by a factor of 100 per cent, it is quite evident that if the Canadian economy is to be ready to respond and take advantage of a potential upturn in the world economy, we must do something to bring wage rate pressures in the Canadian economy under some control.
The New Democratic Party does not feel that is a problem. We on this side of the House clearly do. I know members in this House generally have been crossing the country talking to people and I can say from my own conversations with a variety of people in industry, labour and banking and from conversations with my constituents that wage rate problems are a fundamental factor of importance in the Canadian economy.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
This budget is realistic because it does tackle pressures of cost-push inflation. It does so in a way that does not undermine the restraint program, the monetary and fiscal restraint that we believe is necessary and which if not held would lead to a stoking up of the economy in ways which would be highly inflationary. It is a budget which does emphasize the need for improving the investment climate. It provides in the registered investment shareholders plan and in the incentives for indexed deposit certificates which will encourage investment in the Canadian economy. It concentrates, as my colleague, the minister responsible for housing, indicated to the House earlier this afternoon, an effort on the construction and on the housing side, important not only in terms of meeting housing needs in this country, but important in terms of giving relatively quick stimulation to construction. The budget does focus a relief or a cushioning of some of the impact of higher interest rates in those key areas of the economy where they are most strongly felt.
It is a realistic budget. It takes into account the real world in which Canada must operate. It is a responsible budget. It does not indulge in cloud-cuckoo-land fantasies that there is a quick fix. The budget recognizes the need for restraint. It does make efforts to move us toward new job creation, but in a way which will not increase the deficit. It is concerned, yes, but not panicked by the deficit figures which are projected, because we realize the level of savings in Canada is sufficiently high to finance that deficit and that that deficit flows from a set of temporary factors. It is not, as the United States government deficit is, a consequence of taxation cutbacks and taxation increases in military spending. The Canadian deficit flows from the automatic exercise of stabilizers in the Canadian economy which respond to the recession we are in and which will be overcome as we move out of that recession. Our deficit has not been built in in a relatively permanent way as the United States deficit appears to be.
In talking about a responsible budget, I would like for a few moments to remark upon the arguments presented to us this afternoon by the opposition parties. First, I would like to congratulate the leader of the New Democratic Party on what I think was an earnest and honest speech. There were points in it with which I could not agree, but it seemed to me that the leader of the New Democratic Party did outline, and fairly clearly, major divergences of attitude.
As I said earlier, we do believe the wage pressures which exist at the present time in the Canadian economy are an important factor in the cost-push inflation syndrome. We believe that it is important, through example on our part, that we try and get those wage pressures under control and that other players in the economy, provincial governments and the private sector, respond to the lead that we have given in order that these wage increases which potentially will price us out of international competition will be brought down to reasonable levels. We clearly disagree with the interpretation of the leader of the New Democratic Party in that area.
I listened for some indication in his speech of what alternatives he would suggest. He indicated that he thought we should move quickly to much lower interest rates and that we should engage to a much greater degree in consumer stimulation than we have. What he did not discuss at all-and I hope he will subsequently find the time to do it in a speech here or elsewhere-is how, if we follow that policy, we will be able to avoid the extraordinary, harmful consequences which a similar policy has had within the French economy. The French tried that tack. The result was just recently a second devaluation of almost 6 per cent, an inflation level of 14 per cent and 18 per cent wage increases. The result of what many economists have described as a blown fuse in their economy. Yes, he argued for much greater consumer stimulation, he argued for much lower interest rates, but he did not explain how we would avoid the consequences that a similar policy has clearly had in other economies.
Also he lamented that there was a need to bring forward a clear development and economic planning strategy at this time. What he completely neglected-and perhaps it was because he was unaware of it-was that last November we brought forward an economic development strategy, a document which outlined exactly how we believe those needs should be tackled in the Canadian economy. We have been discussing that strategy publicly and we have been implementing and following the direction which it has charted. It would have been useful in a positive sense this afternoon if he would have given us some indication of those areas of the strategy which he accepts and rejects, and the reasons for doing so.
It is more difficult for me to comment charitably on the speech presented by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Of course, he said-and I suppose it is not an objectionable sentiment-that we should all put people ahead of the party line. That is particularly understandable in his own case because as far as I can discover there is no party line on the Conservative side to follow. The function of an opposition is not just to oppose or criticize. It is also to propose alternatives and to bring forward some views, some strategy or some approach which it believes would be preferable to the path being pursued by government. That, singularly, the Leader of the Opposition failed to do.
I think it was last May 4 that he lamented he had not been able to find an alternative approach to that of the government, that there was not a better solution. Clearly he has not found one since May. There was almost nothing in his remarks which constituted a constructive endorsement of an alternative policy. He did not have a policy on May 4. He still does not have one.
Perhaps I could ask some questions. Does the Leader of the Opposition think that it is courageous to attack suicide? Does he think it is fearless to be against high inflation rates? Does he think it is brave to be opposed to inflation? Does he think he is being forthright when he attacks unemployment? Is the Pope in favour of peace? It takes much more than rhetoric and indignation, feigned or real, to constitute an economic policy.
July 5, 1982

A policy is not what the Leader of the Opposition came forward with today. He is opposed to higher unemployment insurance payments and to cutting indexation. He wants stimulative tax cuts for holders of capital. He is opposed to tax increases for others. Of course, with all that he wants lower deficits. That is supposed to be a policy. He wants more private sector consultation. Then when we bring forward proposals for the registered investment shareholder plan and deposit certificates, he opposes further consultation because of delays in implementation. He wants both more consultation and at the same time immediate implementation. He opposes lower interest rates and then votes in favour of lower interest rates. He opposes FIRA and then he voted for the strengthening of FIRA just the other night in the House of Commons. That is supposed to be policy. What it is quite clearly, to use his own language, is trickery and deceit.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke in the House today for 45 minutes, and in 42 minutes he used rhetoric and attack. He talked about the past, indignation feigned or real, but in his 45 minutes-and I am being charitable now-he used only three to bring forward proposals which he would make. What were his great proposals? What was the policy of the Conservative Party as he expressed it? First, a parliamentary committee to study the estimates again. Second, the encouragement of investment incentives. Nowhere in his speech was there a recognition that the government brought forward proposals to encourage investment incentives. There was no discussion, favourable or otherwise, of those suggestions. There was no proposal as to how they could be improved. There was no suggestion as to whether they might not work. There was no suggestion of alternatives, but a simple suggestion in 45 minutes of his speech that we ought to consider what indeed we considered and what the Minister of Finance brought forward for consideration in the House.
Third, he suggested that we should place greater emphasis upon research and development, apparently unaware that the performance in research and development in the country has shown great improvement over the past two years. There has been an increase from just over .9 per cent of the GNP to now well over 1.2 per cent of GNP devoted to research and development. We are not only well on but are above the track for increasing research and development expenditures which his government charted. There have been increases in the private sector in research and development expenditures of an average 25 per cent per year, exactly because the Liberal government brought forward incentives which encouraged a tremendous increase in the research and development field. Of 45 minutes, less than three were devoted to positive suggestions; those simply slapdashedly stated, not analysed. That was his performance today.
I suggest he has done a real disservice, not only to the House but to the country, in not speaking seriously in terms of analysis, as I must say the leader of the New Democratic Party did, and by not seriously coming forward with some indication of what a Progressive Conservative alternative would be. That he did not do. He cannot complain that he did not have time to do it. We endured 45 minutes of ranting and raving, and all we got were wild charges of deceit and trickery. To have the
The Budget-Mr. Roberts
Leader of the Opposition accuse us of trickery after that speech matches the chutzpah of my Jewish constituent who wanted to be treated as an orphan after he had assassinated his parents.
I should say one other thing. When he went through his analysis of all the things he would like to do, such as decreasing the deficit while of course cutting back taxes and increasing a variety of our expenditures, he went on to complain that the real problem had been that we as a government had not seriously tackled the problems of government expenditure. He has been a member of government, if only briefly, and I suspect that he is aware of the facts. Certainly he should know them. The Public Service of Canada has increased over the past 20 years. It has increased on the average each year by 1.3 per cent. The annual growth of the population over that same period on the average has been 1.5 per cent. Over the past 20 years the growth of the public service has not kept pace with the growth of the population, even though public services have to grow to serve the needs of the population. In the years since 1978, indeed, the growth of the public service has declined at a rate even lower than that. It was a German politician of not great repute who developed the tactic of the big lie. The Leader of the Opposition has developed the tactic of the big panic and attacks rather mythical problems and exaggerates.
He talked about the need to get government expenditures under control. He should know that expenditure by the federal government on goods, services and fixed capital has been roughly constant over the last 20 years or so; indeed, in most recent years it has been declining. It is just over 20 per cent of gross national product. It is quite clear that it has not been extraordinary increases in government programs or government expenditures which have caused economic problems in Canada.
I do not ask him to accept my comments on that. I would just refer him briefly to the June report of the Investment Dealers' Association of Canada in which they provide figures which indicate the relatively static level of federal government expenditures as a proportion of the GNP. It concludes by saying:
Government spending on goods and services has become a less important portion of Canadian aggregate demand. In recent years governments have been making serious and successful efforts to reduce growth in their spending.
What we heard today, when there was an opportunity and a need not only for serious analysis but for a presentation for the alternative view from the Leader of the Official Opposition, was 42 minutes of high school sarcasm and three minutes of non-constructive suggestions.
I said there were three characteristics of this budget. It was realistic, responsible and tough. These were characteristics which were certainly not shown in the speech by the Leader of the Opposition. The budget is tough because it recognizes, admits and communicates to the public of Canada that there are no quick fixes for the Canadian economic situation.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Roberts

It does not attempt to evade responsibility. It admits that the standard of living in Canada will be lowered temporarily and argues that the burden of that lower standard of living should be shared within the country.
Nothing was more ignominious in a pretty ignominious speech by the Leader of the Opposition than his attempt to frighten-I do not know if that was his deliberate intention but it certainly would be the effect of taking his remarks seriously-old age pensioners and those who are greatly in need in our economy by his accusation of what the impact of this budget would be on their situation. I say that, Mr. Speaker, because it is the poor, those who are not as well-off and those who are on fixed incomes, who have the strongest vested interest in seeing the policies brought forward by this budget work. It is they who will most benefit if and when we bring the push for inflation within our economy under control.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment; Minister of State for Science and Technology
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
There has been no recognition on his part that those receiving the guaranteed income supplement, which is virtually half of the old age pensioners, will not have any capping placed on the inflationary adaptation of their pensions, that they will receive what they would have received as an old age pensioner and they would have received as a guaranteed income supplement receiver as if this budget had never been brought forward. Those who will have their incomes capped are those who are not receiving the guaranteed income supplement and those who are not in as great need as those at the lower level in our society.
It is true that this budget does increase taxes. It is designed to stimulate job creation and to help those who are in need, not by increasing our deficit but by increased taxes, so that those who do have income can help with their taxes to create jobs for those who are not so fortunate in our society. The employed will pay more on their unemployment insurance premiums and they will do so because they will be indirectly assisting those who are not fortunate enough to be employed to receive their benefits.
This is a tough budget because it recognizes that we will face the unpleasant fact of high interest rates so long as United States interest rates are high and that unfortunately there is not, as the NDP would like us to believe, a method by which we can lower our interest rates startingly below those in the United States in a quick move to resolve our problems in that manner.
The budget does say that we should cushion the impact of those high interest rates on those who need cushioning the most; those who receive the guaranteed income supplement and those receiving the child tax credit. The budget does say that we should assist farmers, fishermen, small-business men and house purchasers who are those most in need of some relief from high interest rates. However, it accomplishes this in a way which is responsible and realistic. It recognizes that we cannot cushion and insulate everyone in our economy.
I said that this is a realistic budget. It takes into account the real world in which we live. It is a responsible budget. It does not go haring after the impossible, simplistic, dramatic but counterproductive solutions. It is responsible because it recognizes the need to maintain restraint. It is responsible because it does move toward job creation through the construction proposals and it encourages increased investment through the rather inventive and imaginative proposals brought forward for the registered investment shareholders plan and the deposit certificates. It is a tough budget because it recognizes the difficulty of our situation.
It is also a Liberal budget. It is Liberal because it does not just stand aside, as the Conservatives sometimes seem to want us to do, and say: "Let us leave it to the private sector." We acknowledge and recognize that we have responsibilities and an active role to play. We have focused on the cost-push factors which lead to inflation. I suggest it is interesting that both the private sector and certainly the provincial governments as well have reacted to this budget much more responsibly than the members of the official opposition. This Liberal budget recognizes the need to create jobs and investment in Canada by finding new instruments to encourage that investment.
It is not a Tory budget. It is not one which adopts a hands-off policy. It is one that says the government has a responsibility to create a positive and constructive context which will support private sector growth because it recognizes that private sector growth is the motor of the economy.
This is also why it is not a New Democratic Party budget. It does not believe we should abandon restraint programs. It does not believe we should avoid the problems which are posed by galloping wage increases in the Canadian economy. It does recognize the need for the private sector to work with us to generate growth within the economy. It does reinforce the direction which was charted in the economy development strategy a year ago.
It is a difficult budget, one which avoids the excesses which I believe have been presented by both parties on the other side of the House. It is a policy excess on the part of the New Democratic Party and simply a rhetorical excess on the part of the Conservatives. It is a Liberal budget. It is tough, responsible, realistic and deserves the support of the members of the House.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to take part in this leaders' day debate when the leaders are present or have been for part of the time. I am also pleased to hear from the party spokesmen some of the philosophies behind their policies. The hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Roberts) who just spoke for approximately 30 minutes spent about three minutes in defence of the budget and used the rest of his time to attack the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). We sat and endured it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Talk about being hypocritical. He read the polls in his riding.
July 5, 1982

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The only defence I will offer in support of the Leader of the Opposition is that he was only telling the House what the people of Canada are saying to him. That is who the government should be listening to. That is all I will say about that matter.
I believe the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) gave an honest speech. He wired himself thoroughly to intervention in the business affairs of this country. He knows that he is doing so. He is cutting off any chance he has to get the labour vote and he realizes that while doing that he is attempting to maintain the alliance with the government side with its tendency toward intervention.
I suggest that this debate has been worth while. I am more interested, however, in putting on the record the efforts that have been made in the House over the last number of years to put an alternative policy before the people of Canada that is distinctly Canadian, practical, economic and is fitted to today's situation. In other words, I want so speak about the budget in perspective. Over the past number of years we have had in intellectual circles, particularly among economists and businessmen, a debate on the theories of Lord Keynes. That debate reached its peak around the fifties. Many of our senior civil servants became great devotees of this pattern that was going to solve all our problems. I think of men like that very fine gentleman, Bob Bryce. I can think of the deputy minister of finance 35 years ago.
Second, we have had a debate among the economists mostly about the theory of monetarism. There has been a great deal of argument backward and forward. We have seen this theory accepted not only in Canada but in the United States, in Great Britain and in most countries in Europe.
Third, we have had a number of debates of a sundry nature of such things as the Phillips curve where you have to balance off unemployment against inflation. That is all we heard from the civil service 25 years ago. The only persons we hear talking about it today are members of the government who keep going back to their schoolbook knowledge gained 25 or 30 years ago.
We have had a certain amount of debate on Galbraith. He is the humorist who poses as an economist. This is the intellectual level which the upwardly mobile people in our civil service have reached. These men like Galbraith are just bad smells in a mist. They are here, they are there, they are every place, and you cannot put your hand on them.
In the last ten years there has been a series of debates in the United States on what I call, and I think it is the correct phrase, the Mundell-Laffer hypothesis. Mundell is a Canadian and Laffer is an American. All these fellows preached was a common sense approach in economics based on quantitative analysis. If in analysing what was happening in the various industrial countries of the world we saw that what the policy was resulting in was exactly the opposite of what it was intended to do, then common sense would suggest we go the other way.
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
About two or three weeks ago the financial spokesman for the New Democratic Party asked a question in this House. In my judgment, it was probably the most thoughtful question I have heard in this House in two or three years. He asked, in view of the fact that all of the policies the minister is carrying out or talking about are proven failures, would the minister not consider it wise to do just the opposite? At least it would not be any worse than what is happening to us now. That is an Irishman's way of saying, "If I cannot get the cork out, I will push it in." It makes sense. That is exactly what we have been debating here these last two or three years.
We have all the quantitative evidence in the world that certain things that are considered truths under Keynes and the theories of Keynes have become the religion of the guiding lights behind this government. When you have the evidence that these things are not working, commonsense demands you go the opposite way. That is all Reaganomics is, just go the opposite way to what you have been doing.
When I hear condemnations in this House about frightening away the business people, I simply say we should look two or three years down the road. On July 1 of this year the first major move of Reaganomics went into effect in the United States. They reduced their taxes across the board by 10 per cent. In this budget our government increased them 5 per cent, again going the wrong way.
Either on the last sitting day of the House or earlier today, I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) say something that is pure Keynesian. He said in effect that inflation is caused by too much demand for too few goods, demand-pull. He does not realize that one third of our industry is working under a very limited capacity. To put it another way, only two thirds of our industry is being utilized today. The minister fails to recognize that 1.5 million people are either unemployed or partially employed.
We cannot have a demand-pull situation when the factories are full of goods and the mines are overwhelmed with their inventory. Demand-pull is pure Keynesian. Keynes did not know anything about cost-push, yet I heard the Minister of the Environment, the hon. member for St. Paul's mention cost-push. This budget increased the cost-push. Cost are those things that add to the price. The biggest thing used to be the cost of government. In the last two or three years, it has been overtaken by tremendous bursts in the cost of interest. The number one enemy in the last three years has been the cost of interest, then the cost of government, then such things as land costs, and the question of the money supply or monetary theory. Fifth place on the list is labour costs. All this budget does is take advantage of the popular opinion across this country.
It says the first guys that should be clobbered are the public servants. They have seen the example of the other provinces doing it, so they ask themselves, why not do it here. It does not get at the number one, number two or number three basic big costs of cost-push inflation.
We could get this debate on to a high level if the government listened carefully to some of the ideas that have been

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
presented. I am not going to go through them. 1 have been pleading for years to get the debate up to reality. Let us face the fact that the quantitative evidence shows the paradigm or pattern of Keynesian economics has never applied to Canada because it is such a big country. It is not applying to any country. It is not working.
Let us debate the fact that three years ago, in 1979, a budget was introduced by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). It had a tax increase of 18 cents on diesel and gasoline with a tax credit for the person who drove a car. That was the first budget in the history of the western world that tried to get at the budget deficit by decreasing taxes. That has never been pointed out in the House by anyone with the exception of myself.
Across the world it caused tremendous ripples. As I said two or three years ago, in the spring of 1980 The Public Interest, which is probably the most profound and widespread intellectual magazine in the world, put out a special issue entitled "Economic Theory and Policy in Disarray". One of the main articles in that magazine was headed "The dissolution of the Keynesian consensus" by James W. Dean. Let me read six sentences to the House:
On December 13, 1979, the Government of Canada fell. For just six months the Conservatives had governed with a parliamentary minority, and they were defeated on a vote of no onfidence. The issue was their first budget-a budget that rejected Keynesian economic policies, replacing them with radically different recommendations. Unemployment and slow growth were to be fought not by increasing the federal deficit but by reducing it.
This is not a new philosophy. It was tried in a pragmatic way by Mellon, the Secretary of the Treasury under several Presidents of the United States in the 1920s. It was tried by Kennedy from 1962 to 1964. Instead of having a big budget deficit, by reducing the tax he got a surplus, because the demand factor was such at that time that everybody bought the goods, created new wealth and provided enough tax to give him a surplus.
It goes on to say, about the Conservative turnabout:
Their turnabout mirrored that of much of the economics profession throughout the English-speaking world. It was the decade's last dramatic reflection of a dissolving Keynesian consensus. This paper traces how that dissolution came about.
I am not going to read the whole thing but what I have said should be enough to show that the Crosbie budget of 1979, with just six or seven small tax, decreases as a way of balancing the budget-it could not balance it in one year-was a small but important start.
Then the budget we got in 1980 stopped that. I remember my criticism of the first budget of the present Minister of Finance. I said he zigged when he should have zagged.
Then there was that disastrous budget of November 12, in which they went in a completely opposite way to what they had done over the previous ten years. They are creating a whole series of incentives for people to save money and they call them loopholes. That has put the country in a complete panic and in a paralysis. This frightened the government so much that it
even had to recess the House in order to reconsider the budget. They took the brave, stout stand that they were not going to give in. But they gave in in the last part of June, and now they have brought down this budget of June 28.
Instead of learning from the series of mistakes that they made in 1980 and 1981, and heading the wrong way, they added to the costs by increasing the taxes, with no evidence of restraint. In other words, it was a wrong-way budget, but it has served one good purpose. It forced the government members to think.
It is no accident that in this debate minister after minister has got up on the government side trying to defend this budget. They know what the intellectuals think of it, they know what the businessmen think of it, they know what the common people think of it. So they brought in this new budget, in the hope that it would paper over what they thought were the mistakes of November 12. They did withdraw some of the things they did in the November 12 budget. But this is not an economic budget. It is not an accounting budget, it is simply a high tax budget.
They are doing exactly the opposite to what they should be doing. They are still working on the assumption that when you are short of money you tax for it. The truth is that if you want more money, you should lower the taxes, and you will get more money and get the country growing in the process.
I think I have said enough, Mr. Speaker, on the perspective, I think I have said enough on the Crosbie budget. I did not think it went far enough in tax reductions, but at least it was a start. I think I have said enough, if I may use the common phrase for the last three budgets, on the MacEachen budgets. In one case he zigged when he should have zagged; in the other case he brought on national panic and paralysis; and this one can only be described as a budget that brought on stupefaction. Even the Conservative Party members are stupefied. The Conservative Party is stupefied at the immensity of the ignorance that is coming out from the other side of the House. I used to blame this mostly on the mandarins, but I know that the mandarins do stick into the budget certain things which are a contradiction of what we hear, from the floor of the House from the minister.
I never thought that I would hear, in the question period today, the minister talking about a demand-pull type of inflation. He could not spend any more money because there would be more demand-pull and therefore higher prices and more inflation. The hon. member for St. Paul's is right. What we should be looking at is the cost-push. Every time you add to the costs, you force people into the recession, which is now changing into a depression.
We have gone so far into the hole that it is doubtful whether any government could get out of it quickly. So I think the action program has to be, not a single act, or what they call in the modern days of drugs as a single "fix". But there are some things that can be done. They would not hurt the balance of ways and means of the budget or increase the deficit and bring the taxes in, in a year or so.
July 5, 1982

These things can be considered seriously. They are not political. I think that members of all parties can support them. Let us take the sensitive subject of monetary policy as a starting point. 1 think that government, to start with, could first just ask the Governor of the Bank of Canada to be silent on the weekly bank rate. This is nothing but far-seeing psychology to convince bankers to raise rates. No one borrows from the Bank of Canada, so why bother announcing the bank rate each week? Just doing that is a negative thing. My suggestion would not cost anything, but it would take a little pressure off the banks which think they have to follow the central bank.
Second, I suggest that the dollar should be allowed to continue to float. Think of all the billions of dollars we have had to expend in this floating crap game. Banks have many more billions of dollars than we have. No country in the world can compete with the five or six hundred billion dollar available from your Eurodollars and other dollars and will look around for a situation where they can make a dollar quickly. That is all we are trying to do, with the bank interfering with the value of our dollar. We are putting a few pennies into a gambling game when the other fellow has got billions; but these few pennies amount to several billion dollars which we have to borrow at 17 per cent, 18 per cent or 19 per cent, adding to our costs. Let the dollar float. Let the world economy come to our assistance in a natural economic way; and do not put us under the control of the American banking system.
Third, let us work out a money supply formula based on reality. Reality is not just the M-l figures that give the amount in the cash accounts in the banks or the amount of currency. Reality is the combination of money in circulation and the velocity with which it moves. A simple way to discover the velocity is just to do what the banks do; a weekly checkup on the cash flow will tell you how fast money is moving. Because if the money is moving twice as fast as it moved the week before, that has the same effect as doubling the money supply. That, of course, is very important in establishing the inflationary impact, in a quantitative sense, on the supply of money.
You do not have to get into a quarrel with the Governor of the Bank of Canada, you do not have to ask that he be dismissed; just ask him to lay off what he does not know anything about.
On this money supply formula, he knows all about velocity. Let us see if he cannot work out some sort of formula that will give him some indication of when to push forward and when to pull back. He still has all the power under the reserve sections of the Bank of Canada Act.
On the monetary point, these three proposals do not solve very much, they simply ease the restrictions of making adjustments that we have to make in the next year or so.
The next point is on fiscal policy. We have all sorts of ways on the fiscal side-and the government is using some of these in the present budget-of affecting our economic situation. Parliament has amended the Farm Credit Act so that the Farm Credit Corporation does not have to borrow from the
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
consolidated revenue fund but can borrow money and get money by any means. It is in the act. All it has to do is get the permission of the Minister of Finance, but he has not given that permission yet. He is saying, "You have to do it my way", which is to pour public money into a subsidy to reduce interest rates three or four points for those who are in financial straits. The whole industry wants lower interest rates. That is its biggest cost factor. The Export Development Act has been amended in this House, with the support of all parties, to give the corporation the same power to raise money by any means. There is all sorts of money available not only from Canadians at half interest rates-they will provide it-but it is also available in the European market at half interest rates. We can get all the billions we want at 6 per cent to 9 per cent, and we do not need to worry about the exchange value fluctuating. We can cope with that; there is an insurance process already in effect now at Swiss banks. Why was the same power not given to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation? I asked my Liberal friends. We proposed this in the House a year ago. We proposed this to the minister in debate, but he turned it down because he thought the Minister of Finance did not want him to support this type of thing. Why should the people who want houses not have access to money at half interest rates when it is not costing the government anything? Farmers have been given this right. Exporters have been given this right. Why should this not also be done for the small businessman through the Small Business Development Bond?
I would like to go on with more suggestions, and I am watching the clock carefully. I would like to see the Small Business Development Bond restored immediately, and let us get rid of those phrases "financial difficulties" and "in dire straits". It should be for everybody.
Second, I would like to see the saving techniques mentioned in the House over the last two years restored and put back into the Canadian budget. We could do that very simply, and it would not cost the government anything. Let hon. members not give me the argument about tax expenditures. We do not get any taxes if there is no business. We do not lose anything on nothing.
Then I would like to see action on that Conservative proposal of a few years ago, mortgage interest deductibility and property tax deductibility. Every year we could give that poor devil trying to buy his own home a $2,500 to $3,000 deduction from his costs. Let us compare that with the proposal of the government to hand out government money, which is borrowed at 18 per cent or 19 per cent, for one year only. These are proposals which can be demonstrated to produce a potential income to the government. They wipe out all costs and produce a profit. What is the matter with making money through sensible business management on the part of the government?
In winding up my speech I would like to suggest that there are a thousand individual, innovative programs the government could put into place without any cost to the government. In fact, the government would make a lot of money out of them.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. A. Hamilton
These ideas are not new. Some of them were proposed in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs three years ago. One is to allow lending organizations to lend money to people buying homes at 6 per cent. Who would lend money at 6 per cent? Everybody would, if we put in one little sweetener, and that sweetener is that if a person sold his house within ten years for a capital gain, half that capital gain would go to the lender. Let us just figure that out and see how quickly we could get our 6 per cent money. The government is not even into that. All it says is "legalize the contractual arrangement." This would not cost the taxpayer anything. It would not cost the government anything. It is not a new idea. I apply the same principle to business.
Second, in connection with businesses, instead of borrowing money, they should be asked to give an interest in their businesses to lenders in lieu of borrowing. Big companies are forced to do it now. They call it turning from bonds over to equity. How quickly we would get money for small business if we accepted the Stanfield proposal of years ago! Money would flow to small business very quickly if a person could invest $5,000 in a small business and take his returns out as part of the profits, instead of having a fixed interest rate. The same thing applies to the share proposal. If we are worried about unemployment and if companies are worrying about not being able to pay increased wages to keep up with inflation, let them pay extra wages in the form of shares or an interest in their businesses. Hundreds of people are doing it, and they give evidence about how it works all the time. The hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) told the House several months ago that he did that in his businesses.
1 could go on and list many things, but the following is the one I put forward above all things. In all capital intensive enterprises in any country, once interest rates go above 6 per cent, the interest payments become the major cost of running a business. At a 10 per cent level with a long pay-out, 75 per cent of the cost of a business is the payment of interest. Someone said in the House today that at the present time nearly two thirds of the cash flow of all our corporations in Canada-based on the frist quarter-is used to pay interest. Just think what the case would be for new business. That 75 per cent is the minimum. With interest rates now at 15 per cent to 20 per cent it is impossible to do anything. Such projects as the pipeline, heavy oil, tar sands and a national power grid from one end of Canada to the other-all of which we should have had 20 years ago-would become good investment opportunities. It has been pointed out by the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) and others that Canadians do not act.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I was planning to wind up at six o'clock.
I am simply pointing out that all these things which were such a shock to us last winter could be corrected in a matter of months, not by way of big handouts but simply by our saying, "Let's finance them by getting rid of that interest cost". Or, as they say in the trade, "Get rid of your front end loading costs" so that businesses are not loaded down with 75 per cent or 80 per cent of their costs being interest. All of a sudden these things which are uneconomic would become economic, and the government, without spending any money, could get many megaprojects going as fast as we could get the manpower allocated to them.
I thank hon. members very much for listening to me. I have made that proposal in the House for 25 years, and I am still trying. No one argues the economics with me. Some years ago the then minister of energy, mines and resources, the Hon. Donald Macdonald, looked at that proposal with his officials and said, "Yes, it is practical". The then minister of finance, Mr. Turner, said, "Yes". His officials looked at it and said it was all right. Why do we not do it? Now that we are shaken up a bit by the stupid following of wrong-way policies for the last number of years, we are finally forced to think. Let us change that thinking into action. There is not a thing I have proposed today which would cost anybody anything. What I have proposed would just make money for everyone.
I would also like-

speakeroldname: Mr. Ron Irwin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, St. Augustine once wrote:
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish, therefore to determine the quality of a nation, you must consider what those things are.
Because a budget is so important to a nation, it follows that in framing a budget we should first establish what things we cherish and how they shall be peacefully shared.
The process leaves us with a series of questions that must be answered before the budget can be hammered out. How do we control inflation? How do we treat the unemployed? How can we alleviate some of the unemployment? How can we get our tradesmen working? How can we conquer high interest? How can we help manufacturers, farmers and fishermen? How much tax is permissible?
July 5, 1982

The use of tax moneys as a catalyst must be clearly defined and understood. For instance, we do not foster the building of homes in a vacuum. We do so because in our nation it is important that our tradesmen work and our people are properly accommodated.
In this budget we have tried to outline those things that we cherish and how they are to be shared. We have decided that we must set an example, and consequently we have said that next year there will only be a 6 per cent increase in salaries for Members of Parliament and civil servants, numbering 500,000 people, and a 5 per cent increase the year after. We could easily have said, and it probably would have been politically popular, that we were cutting back on the civil service. In hard times it is always acceptable to cut back on the civil service. We could have laid off 10 per cent or 15 per cent or even 20 per cent of these employees, but would that have been sharing?
I do not think so.
1 note that last weekend Governor William Milliken of the state of Michigan went even further than the Canadian government. Michigan's 11,500 unionized secretaries and clerks have agreed to an undisclosed wage cut and a freeze at the new level for the next 16 months. We have proposed a salary increase of 6 per cent, but in Michigan unionized civil servants are saying that they do not even want an increase; that they will take less than they are receiving now as long as they have job security.
Some provinces such as Nova Scotia are following the federal leadership, and some provinces even took the initiative before the federal budget proposals. Members on this side of the House are deeply concerned about the impact on fishermen, small business, farmers and home owners.
We are in hard times, Mr. Speaker; no one disputes that. Within his limited resources, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) provided a budget which has reacted to our concerns.
1 will say one thing about the economic downturn, Mr. Speaker. Each member of this House, from all parties, has learned a lot about budgets and economics and I am sure that each has gone through this budget with a fine-tooth-comb.
1 think the minister knew this, and even though there was a great deal of criticism from hon. members opposite about where the funds are allocated, certainly there can be little criticism about how they are allocated and about the clarity with which this is set out in the budget document. The budget is concise, direct and to the point, and the minister is to be congratulated.
These are hard economic times. I do not want to go back to the election of the Liberal government or to the tenure of the Conservative government. These hard times go back to 1973 and are directly related to the Middle East oil price increase which occurred at that time. Even in 1979 we had been forewarned of 1981 and 1982. In that year the Economic Council of Canada pointed out that the United States economy was expanding too fast. There was excess demand, insufficient savings, high consumer spending, high levels of borrowing, and
The Budget-Mr. Irwin
a large U.S. federal deficit. In 1981 President Carter noted that the Middle East price drain would take $40 billion out of the U.S. economy because of the increase in OPEC prices.
These are difficult times and government alone cannot solve them, Mr. Speaker. Roy Phillips, President of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, has indicated that the role of government is to provide a supportive environment but that the task of turning things around must come from the private sector and that the private sector must not abdicate its responsibility. Mr. Phillips' words do not constitute an excuse for government to abdicate its responsibility. To amplify what he said, I think we must be more cognizant of the responsibility of government. I do not intend to go over every detail of the budget but in a general way I should like to look at some of the proposals contained in it.
I have dealt with the 6 per cent and 5 per cent increases to public servants. T here is one important thing that many members have overlooked, and that is the fact that these increases apply to regulatory boards, in some instances regulating the price of food, communications such as Bell Telephone, and transportation. They are not to be departed from except in exceptional circumstances.
We have tried to buffer senior citizens, so there will be no change in the GIS which will keep up with inflation and there will be no change in veterans' pensions. The child tax credit has been increased. Small business will be able to get loans at 4 per cent less interest than they can now, farmers at 4 per cent less, and fishermen at 4 per cent less. We have indexed term deposits. In other words, you pay tax only on the interest which exceeds inflation on a special type of term deposit. This money will be pooled, $3 billion of it, and provided to new home buyers. One hon. member says we have not done it yet. Let us get on with the budget, pass it tonight and do it. We will provide a fund of $1.4 billion for direct job creation. There will be a $3,000 grant for new home buyers and first time buyers. There will be 100,000 purchasers.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You know that housing prices went up by $3,000 the day you announced it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We will allocate an additional $30 million for a home renovation program. We will provide more low income and non-profit housing. I see hon. members are getting restless; the truth bothers them. We will provide new rules for the Canada mortgage renewal plan under which you do not have to defer your interest to the end as under the old criteria.
There is one particular aspect of the budget process which I find very discouraging. Perhaps it is the role of a vocal opposition, but they have cast a lot of darkness and very little light on the issues. Perhaps that is how democracy works. If the government proposes A, B and C, the NDP comes back and says yes, but you did not do E, F and G. If we do E, F and G, the Conservatives come back and say yes, but you did not do

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Irwin
X, Y and Z. And on, and on, and on. The opposition reminds me of some people I had back in my riding who deal in the gold market. They look for bad news. They will get up in the morning and say, "Oh, there is a war in Iran. Great, the gold market is going up." "There is a war in Lebanon. Great, the gold market is going up." "There are so many bankruptcies. Great, the gold market is going up." "There are so many suicides. Great, the gold market is going up." That is exactly what I hear from that Greek chorus opposite who spend most of their time wailing; unloved, unwanted and usually unnecessary. That may be the role of the opposition, but certainly it is not the role of a constructive democracy in difficult times. Let me deal first with the Progressive Conservatives.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, please don't. You have dealt with them, that is enough.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Only because there are more of them. One writer spoke about the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), the finance critic of the official opposition. He said:
Mr. Wilson talks enthusiastically of 'a program of restraint to reduce the size of the burden of the federal government on the economy' and he talks of going through all government expenditures. But after he finishes with advertising, which he suggests might be up to $250 million of a $76 billion total spending package, Mr. Wilson becomes less specific, sounding more like a nibbler than a slasher.
How true. On November 12, 1981, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre said:
The small business community which enjoyed the Small Business Development Bond over about a two-year period now will have it taken away.
So we changed it, but the hon. member is still not happy. He wanted more for the farming community. Do you remember that? We allocated from our meagre resources-we are into deficit financing-an additional $100 million. The hon. member is still not happy. He wants $500 million, but he does not tell us where we are going to get it, and he wants us to spend less. Do you remember his famous 22 per cent speech? We have extensively augmented our rental housing program in this budget. The hon. member said in November that our program was only minimal. Will he be satisfied with the new budget? Probably not, because he says that we need 220,000 units, not 15,000. But he does not say where we are to get the money. At the same time he bemoans the 22 per cent and the deficit. He now talks about excessive government intervention and red tape. That is when he is not talking about his former days in the stock exchange, which he talks about a great deal. My grandfather came to this country at the turn of the century and worked in a steel mill. He died in that steel mill in an industrial accident. His widow received no help from the government. There were no safety regulations, but there are now. There are more inspectors now, there is now a more humane monetary approach to widows. These things cost money and they are government intervention. My mother was in an automobile accident and was paralyzed for 17 years. There was no government hospitalization plan, no aid for doctors or prescriptions. Today we have all that, and this is government intervention.
The Environmental Fund, an international non-profit organization, recently ranked the world's 150 nations based on
three factors: infant mortality, life expectancy and literacy, which is basically what? How well we are doing in the social sciences, health care and educational facilities. Of those 150 nations, Canada ranked seventh, ahead of the United States, Finland, New Zealand and the United Kingdom. Most of our federal tax moneys are spent on social services, health and education. So what would the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre cut? What social services? What education and health costs?
The Leader of the NDP, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), wants us to help renters and home owners with a massive increase in funding for the housing sector. We propose $3,000 grants, and what did he do? Immediately after the budget he went out and gave a news conference. You all saw it. What did he say? He said, "Well, that is not good enough. All that will do will be to make sellers raise the price". In November he was saying "do it", and last week he was saying it will make sellers raise the price. That hon. member will probably never be happy and I will tell you why, because when he is on the same wave length as we Liberals-and periodically he is- it makes him feel uncomfortable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Darn right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Darn right. I should be thankful for small mercies, because this uneasiness is a hopeful sign. To their credit, Mr. Speaker, the NDP has been consistent on FIRA. In November FIRA was forcefully defended by the former hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood-now looking for a provincial riding somewhere in Ontario-and the hon. member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis). Moreover, the leader of the NDP, reaffirms his party's support of FIRA in "Trufax", a publication of the Better Business Bureau. There has been much criticism of FIRA, but that is basically because people are looking for a scapegoat, people who do not understand economic forces, foreign domination or just do not give a damn. We have backed away slightly from FIRA by loosening up the rules, but as a party we must never abandon the principles upon which FIRA was established. May I remind the House that these principles were adopted by an all-party committee of this House in 1970. How soon we forget. Why did a concept such as FIRA receive all-party support at one time? Well, between 1948 and 1968 approximately 87 per cent of Canada's foreign capital requirements came from the United States. This resulted in 57 per cent of our manufacturing and 60 per cent of our mining industries being foreign controlled. Approximately 80 per cent of that portion was controlled by U.S. companies. Specific industries where American control was particularly high were: motor vehicles and parts, 96 per cent; industrial electrical equipment, 90 per cent; small electrical appliances, 82 per cent; rubber products, 85 per cent; and synthetic textiles, 72 per cent. There has been some improvement in the intervening years but not a significant one.
C. W. Gonick wrote:
Today, for example, between one-quarter and one-third of the goods produced in Canada are exported to the United States. These are mostly resource-based products-pulp and paper, nickel, iron ore, lead, zinc, and the like. Canadian jobs, profits, and prosperity in general are heavily dependent on the growth of
July 5, 1982

U.S. markets for these products. It is well known that Canada has never prospered in the face of a depression in the U.S. economy, has never been able to stabilize its prices in the face of American inflation, and has never been able to eliminate unemployment in the face of a downturn in the U.S. economy.
FIR A is a scapegoat because it is highly visible, but it is not in Canada's best interest to run scared at continued foreign domination of our economy this time. The opposition wants a made-in-Canada interest policy, a made-in-Canada job policy and a made-in-Canada trade policy. I suggest the opposition had better look to the decision process and call for decisions on Parliament Hill and not on Wall Street.
The government must act as a buffer in these hard times. I was a mayor one time. One cuts back on spending in bad times and spends in good times. I say that when good times come back we should start cutting back on our spending and pay some of our deficit. Now is not the time to cut back.
On the other hand, we cannot spend our way out of a recession. There must be some prudence. There must be some middle of the road. France found this out very forcefully. It tried to ignore inflation and economic principles, but it wound up with a 14 per cent inflation rate, and just recently it has had to devalue the franc and implement a four-month wage and price freeze. New Zealand has frozen prices, income and rents for the next 12 months. There is a time when reality must be faced and the reality now is that the pie is only so big and the pieces must fit the whole.

speechtext: Where were you two years ago?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

You should have heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), Mr. Speaker, talking about suicides. You should have heard him talk about the widows. The Tories forget that it was this party that brought in welfare legislation for widows, for children, for the unemployed and for the immigrants. I remember that and I remind hon. members of that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much is the deficit?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Now you are talking a different way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have tried to accommodate the life insurance companies. They seem satisfied with the new legislation. We have tried to accommodate HUDAC. As a matter of fact, the president of HUDAC, Mr. Cyril Morgan, now feels that HUDAC was listened to as far as the implementation of some policies that have helped his sector, which is housing; are concerned. He feels that he was listened to when he brought
The Budget-Mr. Irwin
criticism to this government in November. He has some praise for this budget.
We have tried to listen. We have tried to accommodate. Only time and the economy will tell if we are right.
Let me turn now to the national energy policy. In the oil and gas sector as a result of the national energy proposals there will be 50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990. That is not straggering. I cannot think of a country in the world that has less than that. In Canada we seem to feel that the thing to do is to give away our resources as soon as we discover them. Because of public misperception of this goal usually fostered and inflamed by the Official Opposition, we have decided to slow down the process. The minister has indicated that we are ahead of our schedule and that therefore we can do that.
At the same time, as a reminder to members of this House of Commons, I refer to a recent article written by Mr. David Crane, in which he says that the ten most important foreign-controlled oil companies operating in Canada invested $2.5 billion by the end of 1970 and in the same period received dividends of $4 billion. They also hold 80 per cent of equity ownership in Canadian subsidiaries worth $40 billion, which is not bad for a $2.5 billion investment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which party was in power when that happened?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: These companies have expanded from this base into marketing lead holdings, uranium, manufacturing, copper, coal and the building industry.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the hon. member would just stay quiet for a few minutes, he will have a better understanding of resources.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) says "Drop PetroCan." I say, never.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You guys act like you just took over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Foreign investment in oil and gas has been welcomed by editorial writers and by people throughout Canada for almost four decades. Just check the editorials. For four decades everybody in this country welcomed foreign investment. We treated foreign companies well. They had a fair return, and they have no complaint about this country.
I return to what the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) said, a one-time Liberal. That is the one good thing in his favour. He was a one-time Liberal.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We will make you a one-time wonder.

speechtext:
The hon. member for St. John's West was a onetime minister of finance and a one-time financial critic. What is he now? He is a leadership contender, a man in the lockup, I understand, who still thinks he is minister of finance.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Irwin

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It would be nice to have one.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I thought he is a man who has a certain amount of experience and that I could listen to him. I came to listen to him. But what did he do? He spent precious time in this House personally attacking the Minister of Finance of this party for almost 40 minutes without saying anything. The only flourish he had is that he ended by quoting from the poem "The Ancient Mariner". 1 say that the only bird in this House is a duck. It is a dead duck and it is sitting opposite.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Leader of the Official Opposition spoke today. This proves just how much I suffer because I came and listened. The Leader of the Opposition spoke again about using the provinces as scapegoats, that we are once again using them as scapegoats. Remember the argument used concerning the Charter of Rights? It was scapegoats. He has one argument and he goes with it. It does not matter whether we are talking dollars or rights. It is one argument. I suggest the Leader of the Opposition read the British North America Act, and perhaps the Constitution as well. He will find that the provinces do have significant powers. He will also find out that the provinces spend 75 per cent of the tax revenues in Canada. We spend only 25 per cent. When the Leader of the Opposition says that basically we are drawing them in, certainly we are drawing them in. It is their responsibility. It is everyone's responsibility to cure these economic hard times.
Today the Conservatives said, resign. Today the New Democratic Party said, resign.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are unanimous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How would we govern? We could be governed by the party on my right, which would govern on wishful thinking. We could be governed by the party on my left, which would govern by platitudes. No, we will not resign. Our party has a tradition of hanging tough in hard times. Our party has a tradition of keeping this country together, a tradition of fine social legislation. Every good piece of legislation in this House was brought in by a Liberal government. Hon. members should not forget that. We have a tradition of scope.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
