speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have never seen a socialist quit yet.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We accept these challenges, Mr. Speaker. We are not going to walk way from them. That is what the people expect of us. These are difficult times and this is a difficult budget. But if we pull together, chart our course, stick to our bearings and get on with other things we will reach our destination.
I will end the way I started with what St. Augustine said. He said this:
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish,-
I do not think he had the House of Commons in mind when he said that. He continued:
-therefore to determine the quality of a nation, you must consider what those things are.
Let us decide, let us share. After all the partisanship has passed, I know that it would have been the hope of each and every member of the House of Commons-and if it were not, he or she would not have run in the first place-that our country prosper once again. Let us get on with the job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, finally, after
7.5	months of drift, indecision, confusion and chaos, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has once again addressed himself to the nation's economy. Due to the crisis in confidence which the last budget created, Canadians knew that a new budget was necessary. Asking this same minister to bring in a budget is tantamount to asking the captain of the Titanic to chart another cruise through the icebergs.
Before commenting directly upon the budget, I wish to draw the attention of the House to the sorry economic record of the present Liberal government. Business bankruptcies have soared as a result of the Liberal high interest rate policy. In the first five months of 1982, 4,500 businesses closed their doors; that is a 55 per cent increase from 1980. Farm bankruptcies increased 111 per cent and unemployment has reached 10.2 per cent. Over 1.2 million Canadians are out of work. That calculation is based upon the number of Canadians who have recorded their willingness to work. Thousands more have given up because the Liberal government has destroyed their will even to register as being available for work. Inflation, which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wrestled to the ground years ago, has come back. It is an every day occurrence at 11.8 per cent. In the United States, under an administration which the government loves to deride, inflation has been wrestled to 6.7 per cent. One of the main reasons for the huge gap is the cost of energy. The Liberal Party, which rode into power on the sole promise that it would not increase the price of gasoline 18 cents per gallon, now finds that the price of gasoline has risen 86 cents per gallon and federal taxes are 42 cents of that increase. Those were the things the constituents of Simcoe North told me they were concerned about during
July 5, 1982

the last three or four days. The nicest thing about coming to Ottawa from Simcoe North is returning after watching these monkeys day in and day out.
In December, 1981, the Minister of Finance projected a deficit of $10.5 billion. Seven months later he shocked Canadians and the world with a deficit of $19.6 billion. In any business a vice-president of finance who made a 100 per cent error in projections would be fired summarily, but he remains bland and confused as ever, smiling as he answers questions, while all around him Canadians are losing their jobs, homes, farms and businesses. This deficit will cause untold hardship for Canadians. Interest rates will be forced higher as the Government of Canada competes in capital markets for funds to finance the deficit and approximately $25 million worth of Canada Savings Bonds which mature this fall. The investors who supply those funds will not be impressed by a government which operates on such a high deficit and cannot forecast its financial situation with more accuracy. The high interest rate policy of the Liberal Party is killing Canadians. Home owners are giving up when they are faced with 20 per cent mortgage interest rates, farmers are quitting and going bankrupt for the same reason, small businesses are being forced to the wall.
The measures announced in the budget, with which I will deal later, will not deal with these problems. While thousands of Canadians are faced with foreclosures or are forced out of their homes by power sale proceedings, the Liberal government adopts the old diversionary tactic of offering grants to new home owners or to people buying new homes. While thousands of Canadians are going bankrupt, the Liberal government offers interest assistance to small businesses which will expand as long as they are in financial difficulty. The Liberal depression has caused Canadians to cut back on the purchases of appliances, furniture, cars and homes. As a result, those sectors of the economy are in a slump. In order to purchase those items, Canadians need more disposable income. It is therefore a strange time to increase taxes, but that is exactly what the Minister of Finance did in the budget.
As a result of the proposal by the Progressive Conservatives in 1972, personal income tax exemptions were adjusted annually to take into account inflation. This meant that Canadians would not find that inflation was pushing them into higher taxation brackets and higher taxes. It also prevented governments from benefiting from inflation and collecting more revenue. That is income tax exemption indexing.
In the past Liberals have threatened to abandon this principle of fairness. In fact, in November the Minister of Finance invoked the old hocus-pocus to claim that by maintaining indexing he had in fact reduced taxes for Canadians. No one was fooled then, and they are not fooled now. The 6 per cent limit on the indexing of personal income tax exemptions is a tax increase. It is about time the Minister of Finance admitted the truth. The honourable thing for him to do, if he felt in honesty that he needed a tax increase, would have been to maintain the indexing on exemptions and increase taxes, but once again the Minister of Finance abandoned the straightforward course and adopted the devious route known to all
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
Liberals. It is no wonder the Liberal Party faces a crisis of confidence in the country.
The most unacceptable measure in the budget was the decision of the Liberal Party to fight inflation on the backs of the elderly. Up until the recent decision by the Liberal Minister of Finance, old age pensions kept up to inflation because they were indexed accordingly. The Liberals have abandoned that principle of fairness and equity. The Liberals have decreed that every Canadian receiving an old age pension will fall behind the rest of society. Our senior citizens who have given our country so much will be given a double whammy by the Liberals-once by the deindexing of old age pensions exemptions and once by the deindexing of personal exemptions for income tax purposes.
But days before increasing the taxes on senior citizens through the de-indexing of old age pensions and the deindexing of personal exemptions, the Liberal government looked after its own. On June 17 the Liberals allowed pay increases of nearly 10 per cent for ministerial aides and the political staff of cabinet ministers. This is the government which piously preaches restraint, fairness, equity and untruth, and rushes through this increase for its private staff.
We have 1.2 million Canadians out of work. We have thousands more who have left the work force, utterly discouraged by the failures of the Liberal government. The measures in the budget to address this problem are another Liberal fraud. The Minister of Finance boasts of a $750 million expenditure. Most of that is represented by recycled previous programs. In fact, only $200 million is new funding. But with the misplaced pride of a minister who uses the term "I am announcing, I am announcing", three times within the space of 60 seconds, Canadians are advised that $300 million will be used-I want the House to focus on these words-to create permanent private sector jobs through levered investment incentives. Who in the world knows what that means? The same bureaucrats and the minister who destroyed incentives in the November budget are now going to give us levered investment incentives. That fancy wording comes from a finance minister who stood in the House on Monday night last and made this comment as reported at page 18882 of Hansard, and the same comment is in the printed budget papers-at first I thought it was a typographical error-where he said:
Let me sum up by listing the items on both sides of the balance-
Every businessman in the country, and everyone who knows anything about balance sheets always says "balance sheet". However, here is the Minister of Finance and the bureaucrats who can just talk about balance. He does not even understand that it is a balance sheet which has two sides. This is the man who is leading us economically.
If the Liberal government desires to take tangible steps in the creation of employment for Canadians, it will get out of the job-creation business and out of the levered investment incentives and concentrate on funding training and retraining.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We did.

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Lewis

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Sure you did. Two people came to my office in Midland a week ago seeking funding to enable them to take the registered nursing assistant course for 29 weeks commencing in September. They do not want those fancy words. They do not want these short-term projects. They want assistance while they retrain themselves. They do not want any levered investment incentives. They want legitimate assistance so they can obtain a job. They do not want the smoke and mirrors of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy).
At the same time that we are discussing jobs I would point out that I was shocked on the weekend to hear some civil servant telling me that a job means something that is created for two months. A job is employment that is created for at least one year.
While we are dealing with job creation, we witnessed a further fancy dance by the Minister of Finance when he dealt with unemployment insurance. You will recall how he said, "I am announcing." In the fine print of the budget an increase in unemployment insurance premiums was announced. There was no mention of that or no "I am announcing". The Minister of Finance and the Liberal Party proposes to implement a 52 per cent increase in unemployment insurance premiums for employees and 34 per cent for employers before the end of the year, but there was no announcement. I find that passing strange. Here we have a man who is so proud of announcements, yet he would not announce the increase in taxes. However, we elicited that information from him during question period.
Canada used to be a country in which there was plenty of adequate housing. This housing was available either by renting or by purchasing accommodation. The rents were reasonable and the apartments were available. Houses were being built and sold. We had a strong, viable industry which employed thousands of Canadians. Well, the Liberals have changed all that. The Liberal high interest policy is discouraging construction of apartments, and new home construction is almost nonexistent.
It is too expensive to buy and carry a home. A family income of $45,000 is required in order to maintain the average Canadian home listed in the Toronto Real Estate Board figures. As a result, housing starts have plummeted. After 1976 there were 273,000 housing starts in Canada. In 1981, after a lot of Liberal hard work, they got it down to 178,000. In 1982, with a lot more effort from the minister in charge of housing (Mr. Cosgrove) the Liberals are predicting 148,000 starts.
The housing industry is in the dire straits that the Prime Minister talks about. The unemployment rate in the construction industry is 19 per cent. How does the Liberal government address the problem? The same experts who brought in AHOP have come up with a new plan. It consists of grants for first time home owners and purchasers of new homes. It is predicted that it will help 8,000 people, not the 100,000 to whom the previous speaker referred.
The Progressive Conservative Party speaks for all home owners, not just the people who want to buy a home. There are tens of thousands of Canadians who have worked hard to own a home and are scared stiff that they will not be able to afford to keep it.
I was recently in a bank where a former client of mine approached me to ask if I was still practising law. He was dressed in mechanics overalls. He had his small son with him. I told him that I no longer practised law but that my partners would look after him. He said, "Mr. Lewis, 1 cannot meet my new mortgage payments. I will have to sell my home." Those are the Canadians whom we should be helping. They worked hard to buy homes without the benefit of grants. The Progressive Conservatives mortgage interest and realty tax credit plan would have meant $125 a month, $1,500 a year, to that family as a credit against today's horrendously high Liberal interest rates. It probably would have helped that family to keep their home.
Is it not interesting that the Liberals with a $20 billion deficit and a 42-cent tax increase on gasoline cannot afford to help the Canadian home owners? How they laughed at us when we suggested a $10 billion deficit and an 18-cent tax on gasoline! And yet we would have helped Canadian home owners.
Earlier today we saw one more attempt by the Minister of Housing to apologize for the dire straits that the housing industry is in. He went through program after program. Jobs, cheques and applications flowed from his mouth like a gentle rain from heaven as it has for the past few years. We have had the same nonsense from the same nonsensical minister for two years. While interest rates stayed unacceptably high, vacancy rates shrank and housing starts plummeted. If we were to listen to the Minister of Housing, every Canadian would have to move once a week just to move into all the new homes he has built. There would not be anyone working in anything else but the housing industry because he has employed so many Canadians. He has done all that while everything else has gone for a bath.
I would like to make a suggestion to the minister of housing. One Sunday I was at the opening of the Orillia Royal Canadian Legion building complex for senior citizens. I suggest to the minister of housing that, wherever possible when the government is dealing with social housing, that it be linked with the Royal Canadian Legion. I make that suggestion because that complex was planned and organized, as was the first phase, by Branch 34 of the Royal Canadian Legion under the chairmanship of my good friend, Ed Broomfield and his hard-working board of directors. Both phases were set up by the Legion and run by it with no problems and no civil servants. It all goes on smoothly. The Legions from all across Canada are run in a businesslike manner. They served Canada in the time of war and they have continued to serve Canada since the war. They perform a useful service to Canadians through social housing programs.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader

speechtext:
We are going to end you.
The federal government has dealt with small business in the budget. It is proposing to allocate $400 million in order to reduce interest costs by up to 4 per cent for two years on borrowing by small business to finance new investments and research and development. -The criteria which were set forth in the budget papers are confusing. We really do not know whether or not a business must be going broke in order to receive assistance.
When will the Minister of Finance, the bureaucrats and the Liberal Party understand that a small business facing bankruptcy may not necessarily want to expand. Small businesses may not want to build a new building and fill it with machinery, equipment and staff in the hope that business will come in. That is how the Minister of Finance is running the country. We would all be bankrupt if we did that.
It is easy to become a small-business man under the Liberal government. You just buy a big one and wait. However, we will be saved because the Minister of Finance made a number of proposals in his budget in which he intended to refer these items to an ad hoc committee of prominent Canadians; individuals from the financial and accounting and economic community. I have no quarrel with the people who were named to the committee as I understand it at the present time. However, how could the Minister of Finance and the Liberal Party, with the very outspoken minister responsible for the status of women who claims to be doing such a great job, announce the membership of that committee without including one woman? Not one woman was named as a representative. There is no excuse for that error. The 52 per cent of our population that are women contain many highly qualified financial, accounting and economic experts. They should be represented on the committee. If the hon. member for Kingston and The Islands (Miss MacDonald)-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I suggest there are many competent women who can sit on that committee. Marie Josie Drouin, from Montreal, Gertrude Mulcahy, the director of research of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, and Dian Cohen, a noted economist whom the Grits did not want in the lockup because she will not support the party line. More than one prominent Canadian was missed but mentioned later.
Canadians were amused to learn that the Minister of Finance consulted ex-finance minister John Turner during the preparation of the budget. The question is who should be more annoyed that this fact has been made public, the present Minister of Finance or the ex-minister? There is no question
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
that both the finance minister and the Prime Minister have heard the footsteps of John Turner up and down Bay Street and across the nation for several months. It is no wonder they wanted to have him included in this latest fiasco. Misery loves company.
I want to go on record with respect to the ex-finance minister. The Liberal government faces certain defeat in the next federal election as a result of its repeated failures since February, 1980. Nothing would made that defeat more convincing and more sure than to have the Liberal Party led by John Turner.
In Simcoe North John Turner is known as a Bay Street lawyer who quit. In the midst of the 1975 provincial election campaign, he resigned as finance minister of this Liberal government, and who wouldn't, to make a six-figure income on Bay Street. John Turner is no saviour of the Liberal Party or Canada.
This Minister of Finance has called for restraint. At the same time as they pound their chests and brag about increasing taxes on senior citizens, federal expenditures are rising; $62 billion for 1980-81, $75 billion for 1981-82 and $91 billion for 1982-83. That is restraint. They did not dare go beyond 1982-83.
At the same time as they restrain wages and salaries, they sit stupefied while Bell Canada applies to the CRTC for a 25 per cent increase in home telephone rates and a 35 per cent increase in business telephone rates. CN/CP say they will raise the minimum rate for a telegram by 20 per cent. That is how they operate. There is evidence to suggest that they do not know how to restrain prices within their federal jurisdiction. It was a last-minute addition to the budget. The regulatory agencies which are independent still have not heard from the Minister of Finance and the cabinet as to how they are going to restrain prices to the 6 per cent of the finance minister. There is no directive. What kind of operation is that?
The Liberal government has created a crisis in confidence. Canadians no longer believe that the Liberal Party and its bureaucrats have the ability or the desire to come to grips with the economic problems facing Canada. They have watched failure after failure and have seen promise after promise disintegrate in the same manner as the November budget.
How can Canadians have confidence in a government which predicted a $10 billion deficit in November and seven months later revised it to $20 billion? There have been 36 major and minor changes made on seven different occasions. Business, labour, farmers and fishermen, as well as home owners, have been driven to distraction by the indecision of this government.
In a recent discussion with the media in my riding it has been suggested that a coalition of the three political parties be formed. I personally reject that for several reasons. A coalition government is the same as a partnership or marriage. It must be based on trust. Who trusts the Liberal Party?
Our proposals for economic recovery are well known. The Liberals have none. The Progressive Conservative Party has

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Breau
the trust of the Canadian people. We would be foolish to destroy our credibility through association with the Liberal Party. We have seen what it has done to the New Democratic Party.
Who wants to be associated with the Member of Parliament for York East (Mr. Collenette) who says, "Canadians have a cry-baby attitude, particularly in the Toronto area?" Who wants to be associated with the hon. member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) who says, "People who expect the government to pull the country out of this mess are asking too much?" The Liberals like to pretend there are no alternatives to this disastrous course which is leading this country to economic ruin, but those alternatives do exist. I want to bring them to the attention of this House once again.
The Progressive Conservative mortgage interest and realty tax plan would have meant up to $1,500 for every Canadian family in 1982 as a reduction of mortgage interest and realty taxes. That plan would be implemented now if it had not been for the NDP.
The Small Business Development Bond criteria should be changed back to what they were when the Progressive Conservative Party introduced the concept in 1979. There should be once-in-a-lifetime interest relief to small business. The November 1981 budget should be withdrawn. The National Energy Program should be revamped. Government spending must be reduced to control the deficit and reduce interest rates.
In closing let me say that if the Liberal government does not want to follow a sensible plan of action, it should resign and make way for a government that will do something about Canada's economy, namely, the Progressive Conservative Party.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate this evening. It is a very important debate on a budget that was brought forward last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). It is normal to hear the opposition continue to spread gloom and doom. It is normal to hear that from the Progressive Conservative Party. I mention this because it is important that those Canadians who listen to the debates in the House of Commons be reminded of how hypocritical these people are. They are the ultimate in hypocrisy. I just heard one of their members, the member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) go on for about half an hour, talking about the problems of the country, the problems with the economy. Then he talked about the alternatives. I tried to jot down what the alternatives were.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: 1 will speak slower for you next time.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would like to have people here this evening to share with me what his great program was. 1 noted, that he said he would do away with the direct job-creation programs. Never mind that there are hundreds of thousands of Canadians in poorer communities, in rural areas, where unemployment is high-

-who benefit from these programs. The Tory party, if the member from Sincoe North had anything to say about it, and I am afraid he really would, would do away with these programs.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

They do not like to hear the truth over there, they do not like to hear the facts about their phony programs to help the Canadian people. As to real property taxes, they would permit the deductibility of real property taxes, the member for Simcoe North says. Now, look at the facts. Where are the real property taxes the highest in the country? They are the highest in the larger cities, that is where they are high. It is in Ottawa, Toronto, Vancouver. Has anyone in the Tory party asked his Atlantic members how high real property taxes are in Atlantic Canada? They are very low. What they would be doing Mr. Speaker, is to use the federal treasury to help the rich areas of the country.
Mr. McDermid Read the legislation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

It is a program to help the rich, to use the federal treasury, which the poorer areas of the country need, to help the most expensive areas of the country where real property taxes are high and where you have the most expensive homes.

The Liberal approach, Mr. Speaker, is to use the federal treasury, to use the resources of the country, to help the people.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That was two years ago, the member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) says. Yes, it was two years ago. But the Canadian people have long memories. There are people in this House who are going to tell the Canadian people how hypocritical you can be. On the one hand, on the same day that the member for York-Peel was speaking-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -the member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) was up, crying tears for people on fixed incomes.

speechtext:
That is more than you would do.
The Budget-Mr. Breau

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: She said, "You are going to reduce indexation." Yes, I would for sure. I do not question the hon. member's sincerity. There are a few Tories on the other side who really feel what it is that the Canadian people need, that the needy people need. The problem with the member for Kingston and the Islands and some others is obviously that they have no influence with their party. That is their problem.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is why you are not a minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The former President of the Treasury Board told us last Wednesday what the policy of the Tory party was. He said that this $19.6 billion deficit is a strangler, that it should be reduced, that it should be slashed. Why? Because, he said, the market did not like it, there are people obviously in Bay Street who do not like it. Where are you going to slash it, Mr. Speaker, so as to make any kind of difference? Suppose that you slashed it to zero or to $5 billion, or slashed it to $10 billion? If you slashed it to $10 billion, which programs are you going to cut out-so that the member for Kingston and The Islands will not cry for people on fixed incomes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not noticed anyone over there crying.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that this rhetoric about high deficit, about their caring about people, is a lot of hypocrisy. When they get the reins of power they will try. The first thing they will try to do is reduce the influence of the government.
This budget is a budget that provides leadership in the economy, a budget that says that where the federal government has an influence, and direct power to act immediately in the area of wages, it will act. It will limit increases in wages to the public service to 6 per cent in the first year and to 5 per cent in the second year.
Mr. Speaker, for many people who are receiving social benefits, such as family allowances, old age security, public service pensions and so forth, indexing will be limited, as is the case for personal exemptions under the income tax system, to 6 per cent and then to 5 per cent for the second year. The government is proposing this measure, Mr. Speaker, because it is absolutely necessary to convince Canadians and the country's social and economic agents that it can be done, and that the government truly wants to bring inflation down to 6 per cent, and in order to do so, all Canadians are being asked to make a collective sacrifice.
The Liberal Party's philosophy consists in protecting our country's and our society's resources in order to help those who are most in need of government assistance. Since family allowances have been limited to an increase of 6 per cent, child

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Breau
tax credits will be increased by $50 as of 1982, to compensate for the resulting loss of income to low-income Canadians. This means they would suffer no loss of income as a result of the indexing ceiling on family allowances. Similarly, since old age security pensions will also be subject to a ceiling of 6 per cent, people receiving the guaranteed income supplement and therefore having no other income, will benefit from full indexation, because, although all Canadians are being asked to make sacrifices, the Liberal Party does not want the burden to fall heaviest on low-income groups. That is why people receiving the supplement will benefit from full indexation of both the supplement and the basic old age security pension.
Therefore, when the Progressive Conservative and NDP members are speading stories in the House, in the media and among the public that the government is penalizing pensioners and those whose only income is the supplement and the old age security pension, what they are saying is absolutely false, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Irresponsible!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
People who receive the supplement-and I say this again because it is very important-senior citizens who are retired and whose only income is the supplement, should understand that their supplement and their basic old age security pension will not be affected. They will benefit from full indexation on January 1st and every three months, as before. Mr. Speaker, the budget contains other measures that are very important. Interest rates are high and have been for about two years. It started in 1979, then there was a slight drop in 1980. Afterwards, rates rose and dropped again in 1981, but they are rising again now. We have high interest rates because the American government has opted for a policy whose objective is to bring back all those American dollars that were financing world business. It is a fact that the American dollar has been financing a large part of the industrialized world for some time. The Americans have decided to bring back those dollars. In addition, in the U.S. budget for 1983 which has been brought before Congress, the deficit, with the approval of Congress, will be over $100 billion. Those are the two major causes of high interest rates in North America today.
Obviously, since Canada is experiencing the same inflationary pressures as the United States, there is the same incentive to keep interest rates high, because when inflation is running at 10 per cent, for instance, it is understandable that people want a higher rate of return than that on their savings, because if they agreed to a lower rate, they would be losing on their investment. The Canadian government cannot resolve this problem alone. And if we decide not to follow the monetary policy being applied by the Americans, the cost to Canada will be very high.
And the cost would be a drop in the value of our dollar even beyond that experienced during the past month. Consequently, since the government was aware that interest rates would
remain high, partly because of unacceptably high levels of inflation in Canada and partly because of the monetary and fiscal situation in North America, it opted for bringing in permanent, structural changes to help the groups that are suffering the most from these high interest rates. These groups include first of all, owners of heavily mortgaged homes, a second group includes small businesses and also farmers and fishermen, in other words, people who are productive and are self-employed. The government is proposing to provide direct, tax-free cash grants of $3,000 to all first-time purchasers of new or existing homes. Small businesses wishing to expand or to purchase depreciable property will benefit from an immediate 4 per cent reduction in the rate of interest payable to the bank, which will be in the form of a cheque, a cash payment from the federal government, until this permanent policy, this structural change in the interest rate which I mentioned earlier, has become a part of our system.
The Minister of Finance has proposed a new plan for stimulating investment in residential and commercial construction, which will protect the investor from the effects of inflation. However, since the Minister of Finance wishes to ensure that the concept or philosophy behind his proposal and also the mechanism and the legal means for implementing it are accepted and understood and in order to benefit from the experience of people in the private sector, he has formed a committee of experts that is to report to him by September 30, with a view to setting up a program which, in the long term, will reduce interest rates for residential construction, small businesses, farmers and fishermen from 3 to 6 percentage points.

The proposal of the Minister of Finance to have a system of term deposits which will be insulated from inflation has not yet been understood by the public. The opposition, of course, is not interested in making sure the public really appreciates this because hon. members opposite realize how appealing and popular it will be.
While the system will be complex in its application, it is a scheme to create a new indexed term certificate which would pay the investors tax-free interest on that part of the interest which only reflects inflation. Funds accumulated in this way would be directed to purchasers of new homes and to small businesses, farmers and fishermen investing in new plant and equipment.
There will also be a new registered shareholder investment plan whereby the investor puts his money into a fund which buys publicly-traded common shares in Canadian companies. The important aspect of this is that the capital gains on the shares would be taxable at half rate as before, but only to the extent they exceed the inflation rate.
Because the Minister of Finance wants to have the knowledge and the wisdom of people in the investment community, and also because he wants this very appealing and innovative
July 5, 1982

approach to be well applied to make sure that the mechanics- if I can use that technocratic word-of the system will be smooth, he has instituted a committee of experts which will report to him by September 30. Today he said that he wants this report as early as possible, but September 30 is the latest date, so that he can attempt to implement these measures in this calendar year. These are measures that the government is taking to help Canadians immediately.
Earlier I said that the Conservatives say on the one hand that the deficit is too high and on the other they propose new spending initiatives every day. When we propose to limit the indexation of some very expensive social programs-all instituted by a Liberal government-some members opposite try to play both sides of the fence while those who have power in that party-whenever they take power-say that there should be a tighter fiscal framework, that the deficit should be reduced, and that borrowing should be reduced because the stock market does not like the government to borrow too much. These members tried to play both sides of the fence. They know that ordinary Canadians need assistance from the government. They know that some regions of the country need attention from the federal government. When that party was in power in 1979, we saw how they tried to slash programs that were essential in some regions of the country.
At this point I should like to deal with an aspect of the economy and public policy which bothers me, Mr. Speaker. I am disturbed when I hear some members of the public and of the Conservative Party talk about the negative effects of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. They say that investment in Canada has decreased because of FIRA; that we should do away with FIRA or that FIRA is a bad thing. It may be a good thing or a bad thing, Mr. Speaker, I will let history decide that, but I know on which side of the issue I stand.
Let us look at the facts of the situation. When it is said that because of FIRA there is no new investment in Canada, attention should be paid to how much new capital was coming into the country before FIRA was established. When the doors were wide open, there were no screening mechanisms that would make sure that Canadians had a chance to bid on the procurement of foreign-owned companies that had their head offices elsewhere. How much new capital was coming into the country at that time? In 1970 only 8 per cent of total business fixed investment was new foreign capital in the country; in 1971 only 7.6 per cent and in 1972, 4.7 per cent. There was no FIRA at that time.
What happened was that foreign owned companies, particularly American companies-because they had a larger market in the United States, because they were larger organizations, because they were modelled on the branch plant economy- would come to Canada, take over a Canadian company and make it into another branch plant. In most cases they were coming to Canada and borrowing money from Canadian banks in order to take over Canadian companies or to start new ones. In 1970 there was 8 per cent new direct investment; in 1971,
The Budget-Mr. Breau
7.6	per cent; in 1972, 4.7 per cent; in 1973 5.1 per cent and in 1974 4.2 per cent. The idea that, if FIRA were disbanded, all of a sudden there would be new investment coming to Canada, is not true. Instead, American companies, in particular, would continue to come to Canada, buy companies with money borrowed from our banks, probably because they could convince the banks in those days that they had better management expertise or probably because of the volume of business they had in the United States.
One of the things that FIRA does is assure that, with a new corporation or with a take-over, Canadians will have a chance to bid on the procurement of the company. Formerly a lot of American concerns in particular, would come to Canada and not even give Canadians a chance to bid on Canadian companies. Surely we cannot accept that.
When people talk about the horrors of FIRA I wish they would look at the facts and see how much new investment was coming to Canada as a percentage of Canadian business investment in those days. The figure was not impressive. Foreigners were using their management expertise to convince our banks that they were better than Canadians so that they could borrow Canadian savings from Canadian banks.

Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I wish to emphasize that the government is determined to move this country from the world of 12 per cent inflation to the world of 6 per cent. To achieve this, we shall all have to make sacrifices. The federal government is acting immediately in an area over which it has direct jurisdiction, namely, the federal public service including federal members, senators and ministers, whose salaries will be increased by only 6 per cent instead of 11 per cent, and by 5 per cent the second year. In the federal public service the same rules will apply. The government also expects the private sector, which since August, September or October, when inflationary pressures started to be felt in Canada, has been telling the government to show some leadership, to show that it is capable of reducing inflation. I hope that these ladies and gentlemen will understand the government's message and realize that the government means what it says. I hope the private sector will follow the government's lead and reduce wage increases to more sensible levels. Of course 1 expect the New Democratic Party and the unions to protest loudly that it is unfair to set a 6 per cent ceiling on salary increases in the federal public service.
We should, perhaps, remember that the vast majority of federal employees, I would say 90 per cent, have complete job security. Whether the economy is in good shape or bad, these people keep their jobs. It is a different story for people working in the private sector. There, people are laid off-1 agree that in some cases, it is for a very short period, but in many cases, these are permanent lay-offs, Mr. Speaker. The New Democratic Party will always say it is unfair. Of course, but whom does the New Democratic Party represent? It represents the big unions. It wants people in the public service and in the

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Breau
private sector who have strong unions to go on having extravagant wage increases of 10, 11, 12 and 13 per cent, and others working in the private sector who are losing their jobs and have to live on unemployment insurance for part of the year, to be satisfied with no increase at all, in some cases. And that is what is happening in the real world today. So, Mr. Speaker, when the New Democratic Party talks about social and economic justice, we must not forget the people it represents. In Ontario for instance, it supports the United Auto Workers, a union that is claiming that despite the fact that there have been wage reductions or ceilings on wage increases in the automotive industry in the United States, in Canada they are not prepared to make such concessions. These people will continue to negotiate for 10, 12, 13, 14 or 15 per cent. Who is going to pay the shot, Mr. Speaker? People working elsewhere in the private sector, who, in some cases, are not unionized and have to live on unemployment benefits for part of the year. They will have to work to pay the wages of people who have jobs-1 do not begrudge them that-just because they have big unions and work in safe industries. In fact, they work 35 or 37 hours a week and would scream at working 40 hours, while other Canadians have to pay for their wage increases. So, Mr. Speaker, the federal government must lead the way in this respect, and that is what the government has proposed to do in last week's budget. That is why this budget deserves the support of Canadians and of the House.

speechtext:

Does he not admit that that already can happen, that people can borrow on their mortgages, invest the proceeds and write off all the interest?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

The record will show that what I said was if you have a mortgage interest and real property taxes deductibility scheme in the system, that would be an incentive to home owners, particularly the richest ones with the most expensive homes in the most expensive areas of the country, to go out and borrow money and deduct that from their ordinary income and invest it elsewhere.

The Conservative scheme would permit the deductibility of real property taxes and mortgage interest and would be an incentive for people to use that money, not for investment but maybe to go on a trip around the world or perhaps buy some property in Florida. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member during his speech indicated the equity and fairness in the government's guidelines for public service wage settlements. Was my understanding correct that he said he considered it to be fair that a person making $15,000 a year was going to have his or her increase limited to 6 per cent, and similarly the people making $60,000 a year and up were also going to be limited to a 6 per cent increase? subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not use only the figures that the hon. member did, but I said that the system the government had designed was a fair one because in order to start being selective about what increase you would give at what level, as we did with the Anti-Inflation Board-which the hon. member's party opposed in any event-but for this kind of system which applies to the federal public service only and is not intended to be a comprehensive wage and price control program, where there is no Anti-Inflation Board to look at every contract that is negotiated, I say that this is a fair system. I would rather that all government programs and all government initiatives be applied more equitably. Equity is a good and laudable objective, but this kind of program was designed to be administered very simply. It is simply an extension of contract at a given time, and in order to be selective, as the hon. member says, in order to achieve more fairness, it would have meant a bureaucracy such as we had with the Anti-Inflation Board, which would be undesirable.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, surely what we are debating here this evening, as we have been since the budget and as we will be for the next few days, is more than a question of a budget per se. Rather, it is the whole question of a crisis of confidence that the Canadian people have in this government. It is this total lack of confidence which Canadians feel because the government cannot do anything toward achieving a reasonable solution to the problem of interest rates, or the falling dollar. I have never seen anything in my constituency which has unsettled Canadians as much as seeing and hearing daily about the state of our dollar. While not everyone understands the reason for it, it certainly has had a tremendously destabilizing effect on the confidence of Canadians in our institutions. It was a restoration of confidence, Mr. Speaker, as
July 5, 1982

much as anything else, that most Canadians, along with us on this side of the House, were looking for and hoping for last Monday night. Obviously that has not occurred. Canadians just do not think this Liberal government is managing the economy the way it should. Economists do not think so and most writers of newspaper editorials do not think so.
It is this crisis of confidence, Mr. Speaker, that we should be addressing this evening in our debate because it has the greatest potential to do damage to this country. If Canadians generally start to lose faith in their government, they really have no other place to turn to, and this is what is happening at the present time. We see this crisis of confidence and the fact that it was not addressed in any way in the budget, and we also see little things starting to seep out of the government, the cabinet and the bureaucracy which heighten this crisis. Small things in terms of dollars, but large things in terms of the destabilizing effect they have on the public's view of their politicians. As has been noted before, things like the 10 per cent increase given to political assistants of cabinet ministers shortly before the cabinet brought down its budget limiting pay increases to 6 per cent and 5 per cent. This is the kind of thing which has a damaging effect on the fabric of this country, and it is the kind of thing which people are going to remember for a long time. They feel the government has been hypocritical and is maintaining a double standard. That has had as damaging an effect on ordinary Canadians as anything 1 can think of.
Certainly, Mr. Speaker, other countries are in trouble. But if you look at the figures, Canada is suffering more than most, and certainly more than it should. We have a fantastically tremendous potential, and it is literally going down the drain because there is absolutely no economic direction from the present government.
We have a great potential and we are not using it in any way, shape or form in the way we should. Personally I think, and more people are thinking this way, that the government has set Canadians up for wage and price controls this fall. In my opinion, there is absolutely no doubt that this is what we will have. The scenario is there. The government has indicated to the public sector, a sector that it can control if it wants to, that it is imposing limits on the public service. The fact that labour unions do not appear to go along with the government will give the government leverage to return in the fall and bring in wage and price controls.
I think literally we will have the worst of all possible worlds if the scenario I have painted takes place. We are beginning very slowly to see the American economy starting to come out of its prolonged recession. Housing starts last month were up just a little, but they were up. Automobile sales were up just a little, but they too were up. There is some indication that items such as copper, which is used extensively, in cars and homes, is starting to increase in price in terms of building its own base-price mechanism on the commodity exchanges. But I fear that we will find ourselves-because the government has no idea where it is going and has no economic direction-in a situation this fall that while the American economy starts to move up
The Budget-Mr. Murta
and move out of the recessionary period, we on the other hand will find ourselves locked into wage and price controls that will be totally unacceptable.
Traditionally this country has been approximately six to nine months behind the American economy. It is the structure of the economy and the proximity we have in terms of the amount of trade we have with the United States, and they with us, that has put us in that general category. At the present time, we are about 18 months to two years behind the United States with regard to an economic upturn. I am worried that as the American economy comes out of its recession late this fall Canada will go into a wage and price control situation and that when we finally come out of this wage and price control period we will be in such a poor competitive position because the economies of central Canada will literally be in a shambles. The only thing we will have to export in any great amount will be our agricultural products, specifically and primarily grain from western Canada. That is a very bleak scenario. However,
I am almost assured that it will take place. I think it will be disastrous for the country. It will be the wrong direction for us to go, but nevertheless it will be something that all Canadians will have to learn to live with in the future.
What are we looking at presently? What are we looking at in terms of the economy? What are we looking at in terms of a fiscal overview? We have heard lots of charges and counter charges in the debate on the budget over the last few days. Revenue projections for this year have fallen from the November forecast, and these are the government's own projections, of $65 billion to $58.6 billion. The expenditure projections have increased from $75.5 billion to $78.1 billion. As a consequence, the projected deficit has jumped from $10.5 billion to $19.6 billion, or just about $20 billion. Those figures have risen in the space of just seven months. These are the projections which the government made at that time.
The projected financial requirements have jumped from $6.6 billion to an astounding $17.1 billion. The worrisome part is that this $19.6 billion deficit is only an estimate. It is based on the fact that the third and fourth quarter figures, which usually fall, will pick up. I do not think this will happen. 1 would like to see it happen, but there is absolutely no indication that it will. That is why I believe the concept or the scenario of wage and price controls will, unfortunately, become a self-fulfilling prophecy. The deficit will probably be in the neighbourhood of $25.1 billion rather than the $19.6 billion that we have been told will be the case according to the present budget.
Over the past number of months we have seen the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) castigating the United States for the size of its deficit, the handling of its economy and the fact that most of what is happening to us is the fault of the United States. If, however, you take into consideration the size of the projected U.S. deficit of approximately $100 billion and you also take into consideration that the United States economy is about ten

July 5, 1982
The Budget-Mr. Murta
times larger than the Canadian economy, and if you project that on top of what we have as a deficit of about $20 billion, and if the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance and Liberal cabinet ministers were running the U.S. economy, they would be looking at a deficit of $200 billion plus.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I will at the end of my remarks.
Because the United States economy is some ten times larger than our economy we would be looking on a per capita basis at a budget deficit of $200 billion if we were operating the American economy. This deficit will have one immediate dramatic effect. It will drive up interest rates. It is another question in terms of a crisis in confidence. Canadians saw interest rates reach all-time highs this past winter. We have seen interest rates drop. They did not drop as much as we had hoped they would but they have eased somewhat. In my opinion, we are about to see interest rates move up again because of the borrowing that will have to take place. This borrowing will have to take place not only because of the Canadian deficit but also because of the U.S. deficit. The demand for money in the marketplace is fuelled basically by governments going to borrow. This borrowing will have a tremendous effect in terms of pushing up interest rates at a time when most Canadians are keeping their fingers crossed hoping that interest rates will ease and drop. We have truly a very bleak picture for our economy. Admittedly, it is bleak for other countries, but in comparison it is probably worse for Canada than for any other country in the world. That is evidenced by the kind of confidence that outside investors have had in this country, for instance, the way the market has discounted the dollar against other currencies and a number of other things that have happened.
We are in for a very long, dark and dismal economic situation at the present time. The budget projections for the economy-and these are the minister's own projections for this fiscal year-indicated in November, a few months ago, that in 1982 the real growth in the economy would be approximately 2.2 per cent and that employment would grow approximately 1.6 per cent. We were told that the unemployment rate would be about 7.8 per cent and that inflation would rise to 11.7 per cent. In less than seven months the Minister of Finance returned and told us that we would have a drop in the real GNP of about 2 per cent, almost exactly what he forecast, the worst record of any OECD country, and that the unemployment rate would be 10 per cent. He also indicated that despite the oil glut and lower than expected food prices, inflation would remain at approximately 11 per cent. In the November budget, inflation in the United States was projected at 8.7 per cent, and it ran at 7.2 per cent in the first five months and at
6.7	per cent in May, compared with 11.8 per cent in Canada. This is one of the main reasons we are seeing our dollar drop, and it will be another reason for seeing interest rate increases.
We are not in the same league with most other major producing and exporting countries of the world.
The projected negative growth rate in the economy of minus 2 per cent is the worst since 1946, so no wonder Canadians do not have confidence in the government, in the Prime Minister, and in the Minister of Finance who really do not know the direction in which they are heading.
If one looks at the over-all budget, there are winners and losers as there are in any budget. I suppose the winners, if one wants to call them that, would be low-income couples with children and single parents who would have been receiving the refundable energy tax credit for two years. They will benefit from the $50 increase per child in the child tax credit, but this will be partially offset by the indexing of family allowances and income tax brackets. With somewhere between $12,000 and $15,000 of earned income, even these people end up being net losers.
Another winner would be small businesses which are able to finance scientific research and the purchase of depreciable property. They would benefit from the rebate of up to 4 per cent on interest rates, but basically it is a partial restoration of the Small Business Development Bond that was gutted by the Minister of Finance in his November budget.
Farmers on the verge of bankruptcy can also obtain loans and partial interest rate rebates to help them survive, but most of this money comes from funds which would have gone to farmers in positions to expand production. Even with the small business development bond concept, we will not find at this time many takers.
If one expands one's business, to whom will one sell it? Canadians do not have the confidence right now to purchase appliances, cars or homes. If they have money or any surplus in their disposable income, most of it will go into savings because they are not sure and are concerned about where we are going.
Basically that ends the short list of beneficiaries in this budget. The losers include virtually every taxpayer-all married taxpayers without children and all married taxpayers with children earning more than $12,000 per year. These people will pay more as a result of the partial deindexation of the income tax system. This will mean $1.7 billion in additional personal income taxes to the federal and provincial governments in the remainder of 1982-83 and in 1983-84. That takes in a lot of Canadians, virtually all Canadians.
Another loser will be old age pensioners who are ineligible to receive the guaranteed income supplement. As an example, single people with total incomes above $8,500 per year and married couples with total incomes above $14,300 per year will receive $80 less per person or $160 per couple in 1983-84 because of the 6 per cent cap on indexing in 1983 and the 5 per cent cap in 1984.
They may also have to pay more income tax because of the partial deindexing of the income tax system. Meanwhile
July 5, 1982

upper-income earners, people who earn more than $30,000 per year, continue to enjoy the full benefits of reductions in marginal tax rates in the November 12, 1981, budget. All high-income earners and employers will also likely be hit with a substantial increase in unemployment insurance premium rates. Low-wage federal public sector employees will also be losers. They will be subjected to the same restraints as those in the upper income ranges who will retain the benefits of the November reductions in marginal tax breaks.
Who else will lose? One group is the native people because the spending of government in this regard will be reduced by some $80 million over the next two years. This is spending by government on economic development for native people. It will mean higher social costs in years ahead to meet the needs of this group, perhaps the most economically disadvantaged in the country. While it appears we are saving $40 million a year on one hand, the cost could very well be much greater than that in the next two years.
The huge increase in borrowing requirements will translate into further downward pressure on the dollar and further upward pressure on interest rates. This will mean higher prices and delayed recovery, hurting both consumers and the unemployed. Virtually everyone in the country loses because of the budget. The people who could be considered winners are not really winners because they do not have the confidence they should have in the Minister of Finance, in the Prime Minister and in cabinet.
To sum up, the budget contains no measures to provide job creation or to stimulate lagging consumer demands. There are absolutely no projections in terms of unemployment or what we are to expect in coming months. There are no projections in terms of wages. The budget provides no projections in terms of investment. There are absolutely no economic indicators for 1983 to give Canadians, money markets, stock markets and investors some indication as to where we are going.
The budget is also sadly lacking in that it does not instil confidence in Canadians. Until that takes place we will find ourselves wandering aimlessly as a country, a country which at one time was viewed as one of the centrepins of economic stability with a good standard of living, a country which in the last few months and years has come under a cloud of suspicion as more and more people ask whether Canadians know what they are trying to do, whether they know the economic direction in which they are going, or whether the government really cares. That is the saddest part about the budget. It indicates to all Canadians that the government really does not care.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-COSTS OF DORVAL. (B) POSITION OF AIRLINES
AIRPORTS-COSTS OF DORVAL. (B) POSITION OF AIRLINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 28, at page 17869 of Hansard, I asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) a number of questions relating to the rumours that were then circulating about a transfer of domestic air traffic from Dorval to Mirabel. This question had already been broached in the House by my colleague for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) as well as other members who also raised this very matter.
The matter of concern on both sides of the House was a proposal to shift from a self-operating and self-supporting airport which was actually making money-Dorval-to one which is limping and had been limping along for a number of years. The obvious intent was to spread the blessings somewhat-perhaps not blessings-which may be making them both run into the red, being one of the problems.
There is not enough time to go into the history of Mirabel this evening. I think perhaps you know about it as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, so I will not go into the history. However, some of the related matters are of considerable interest.
One of the questions I put to the minister on that occasion was whether any of the domestic airlines had literally asked to be moved from Dorval to Mirabel. The answer to the question was no, there were none. Not one domestic airline had asked for the privilege of moving from a well operated airport which had all the communications with the rest of Canada very well organized. Not one operating firm asked to be moved to the other airport.

July 5, 1982
Adjournment Debate
At about that time there was an article in the Gazette following a press conference given by the Minister of Transport. I believe he was in Montreal at a ceremony connected with the port of Montreal at that time.
The press had asked him a few questions about Mirabel. Ele then outlined that there seemed to him to be only two alternatives. One was to transfer all Dorval flights to Mirabel except for flights within Quebec and flights to Toronto; presumably to and from, but I am not sure about that. The newspapers only say "to". I wonder if it is clear to everyone what this would mean. It would mean that all internal flights in the province of Quebec would go to Dorval and that flights to and from Toronto would go to Dorval. All other flights headed for Montreal and area would land at Mirabel. 1 do not know whether you have had any experience with Mirabel in landing from overseas flights, for example. I certainly have.
We were delayed on departure from the other side of the ocean and I suspected, because of the forecast arrival time, that when we arrived there would not be any transportation. We were to arrive at approximately 11.30 or twelve o'clock at night. I sent a note to the captain of the aircraft and asked if he would be kind enough when he was in voice contact with Mirabel to arrange for a bus to be waiting to take those of us who were bound for Ottawa from Mirabel back to Ottawa. This was a chartered flight. Happily I did that. When we arrived at Mirabel, there was not a single transport vehicle in sight; not a taxi, not a bus. The parking lot was empty as well. We could not even have stolen an automobile on that occasion. The bus was waiting. The bus driver was not too sure how to get to Ottawa, except by going to Montreal and then on to Ottawa. He could have cut across country, but he was not familiar with that route, and maybe he did not want to cut across country at that time of night. There were eight, ten or twelve of us on that flight who wanted to come to Ottawa. That was two years ago. To this day I do not know how the people got to Montreal. They may still be trying to get to Montreal by their thumbs.
I see, Mr. Speaker, you are signalling that there is a time problem. I can appreciate that.
I made a suggestion as to how to avoid involving the Canadian people in expenses of that sort. The minister strikes me as being very much like Mr. Micawber, the eternal optimist who thinks that something is bound to show up. In his press conference he said it might be possible the resulting increases from Mirabel would bury the issue. He was hoping that the decision could be delayed, primarily because the government was waiting for an upturn in the economy. This is where the "Mr. Micawber" aspect of the minister comes in. The minister might even conform to the G. K. Chesterton definition of Mr. Micawber when he said:
-the preposterous and sublime victory of the human spirit over circumstances.
He felt 'that perhaps the human spirit was great enough, perhaps a little bit like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen). It is catching because they sit across the aisle from
one another. He feels that circumstances will improve matters and it will then be feasible to move the traffic from Dorval to Mirabel.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that Mirabel stands as the forty-seventh airport in Canada as far as traffic is concerned, while Dorval is in the neighbourhood of fifteenth. It has maintained that position over the last three or four years. By comparison, Vancouver is second or third, and Victoria is twelfth or fourteenth. Victoria still does not have radar.
I suggested to the minister that rather than transferring the traffic and incurring another debt, he might use the funds he was planning to use for the transfer to instal radar at Victoria international airport. The thirteenth or fourteenth airport in Canada could then enjoy the benefits of that facility.
