The second point I would like to strees is that it is wrong to assume that a pot of money will suddenly become available if the government decides not to transfer flights from Dorval to Mirabel. On the contrary, should the decision be taken to make the transfer, one of the major considerations will be where to find the necessary funds. There is an almost unlimited demand on the limited funds available for airport improvement across the country.
The opposition deplores the great deficit, but, when it comes to a local project of interest in an individual member's riding, there is always great enthusiasm for more spending. The hon. member might recall the expenditure at Victoria airport last year on an instrument landing system amounting to a total of $1,644,600. That was spent right in his own riding, Mr. Speaker. Let us not hear specifically from that member, deploring the great deficit while at the same time wanting millions and billions for his riding.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROLS- GOVERNMENT POSITION-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE ESTIMATES
THE ECONOMY-FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROLS- GOVERNMENT POSITION-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 21 1 had an opportunity to put two questions to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), Acting Prime Minister in the absence of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). One question was with respect to any potential intention of the Government of Canada to impose foreign exchange controls. Another question related to an examination of the estimates by a special committee of the House.
In response to the first question, which I thought had some significance, the minister suggested that 1 discuss the matter in the debate which was to follow that day. The fact of the matter is that the question was raised because of an unsatisfactory response by the Prime Minister to a similarly worded question by the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) a week earlier.
Since the date of that initial question and the unsatisfactory response, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian dollar has been consistently bombarded and reduced substantially in level of value vis-a-vis the American dollar, to the extent that it dropped below where it was earlier today. That decline has not been substantially remedied. I would have thought that any Prime Minister, or Minister of the Crown acting as Prime Minister for the day, would have relished the opportunity to dispel any concept that this country had become a banana republic, imposing foreign exchange controls where its own financial control had gone completely awry. That opportunity was not taken, much to my dismay and, I am convinced, to the dismay of many Canadians who might have feared that their opportunity to convert Canadian dollars into other currencies would come to an end very shortly.
In any event, since that time the minister has introduced his budget. Once again, fortunately, there was no provision for foreign exchange controls therein. If we wish to protect the value of the dollar, surely it is incumbent upon government to indicate in a very clear and unequivocal fashion to the general
Adjournment Debate
public that it has not sunk to the level of those states which have lost control of their financial affairs.
The second question I asked was a legitimate question, designed to take from this House and submit to a committee of the House the opportunity to examine the estimates. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that there are members on the government side, just as there are members on this side, who are personally aware of waste and extravagance in government expenditures with which they would very much like to deal in an effective manner. They cannot deal with them in an effective manner in this House; they could have in a committee. Not only are there specific illustrations of waste but there are also circumstances in which, with prudence, expenditures of government may in fact be cut. I would have hoped that process might have got underway.
A multitude of substantial expenditures were approved in the budget of November, 1981, and again confirmed in the most recent budget, which, in my view, are the last vestiges of the days of wine and roses of this government. To spend $1,724 billion on foreign aid, and in the current budget to proclaim that these expenditures should increase by some $36 million- that appears at page 16 of the budget papers filed by the Minister of Finance-is reprehensible, having regard to the fact that those same budget papers make provision for the reduction in old age security payments of $5 million this year and $100 million to our senior citizens next year.
Because of this country's economic circumstances the time has come for the government to recognize that its primary obligation is to the people of Canada. If there are in fact excess funds available, those funds should be allocated to Canadians. We can no longer enjoy the luxury of spending our money in a foolish and reprehensible fashion. The Canadian public is aware of the circumstances which face them daily when they lose their businesses, their homes and their farms. If funds are available, and the government makes up its mind as to what funds are available, I think the funds should be used within Canada.
A closer examination of a variety of projects might be undertaken, but we are denied that opportunity because the government is fearful that if it refers such matters to a standing committee of the House for examination, the committee would produce a report which would be meaningful and result in the reduction of expenditures.
If the government really intends that people should lower their expectations, 1 submit it is the obligation of the government to do the same. It should not increase taxes; it should not increase expenditures; it should lower its own expectations. The public learns better from example than from exhortation, and that example has not been provided.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-FOREIGN EXCHANGE CONTROLS- GOVERNMENT POSITION-REQUEST THAT SPECIAL COMMITTEE EXAMINE ESTIMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me once again to be able to say that the

July 5, 1982
Adjournment Debate
government has no intention of bringing in foreign exchange controls. We do not intend to adopt that kind of magical solution in any of our economic approaches to Canada's current difficulties. In fact, in our budget we have stressed that we want to take a disciplined, long-term approach to Canada's inflation problems.
If we look at page 3 of the budget papers, we discover what has been happening to currencies all over the world between 1979 and June 24, 1982. In that period the Canadian dollar declined against the American dollar by 7.8 per cent, but other currencies declined against the American dollar as well. Let me give some examples.
The British pound declined 9.6 per cent; German money declined 9.5 per cent; the Japanese yen declined 13.9 per cent; the franc declined 16.7 per cent; and the Swiss franc declined 15 per cent. Currencies all over the world have declined in value against the American dollar. In fact, Canada's currency declined the least during that period.
Why is this decline going on at all? First, it is happening because Americans have come to grips with their domestic inflation, and there is less erosion of money inside their country. Capital from all over the world is attracted by that characteristic. Second, the United States has continued a policy of very high interest rates, and that acts as a second magnet. We ask Canadians to realize that exchange controls and other magical answers will not respond to that. We need the long-term discipline underlined in the budget to battle inflation and to bring down our own interest rates.

subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATION COMMISSION-RATE INCREASES GRANTED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY. (B) EFFECT OF COMPANY LAY-OFFS ON UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUND
CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATION COMMISSION-RATE INCREASES GRANTED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY. (B) EFFECT OF COMPANY LAY-OFFS ON UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to raise the question of B.C. Tel and its flaunting of both the unemployment insurance program and the CRTC. On June 30 I requested that the government, through the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fox), instruct the CRTC to withdraw a substantial portion of the rate increases granted to B.C. Tel over the past two years. I asked this because B.C. Tel is planning to lay off over 2,000 employees throughout B.C. for up to six months. This will allow its services to customers to deteriorate even more seriously than they have already.
The CRTC has always made as a condition of rate increases the improvement of service to customers. I must criticize the CRTC repeatedly. For example, not very long ago I pointed out to the CRTC that it was taking this company over 30 days to meet the demand for new installations. But the service has not improved, Mr. Speaker, and now it will worsen even further as a result of the lay-offs.
B.C. Tel flaunts the CRTC and makes a mockery of it. It knows that the 2,000 employees are essential if it is to fulfil the charge that the CRTC has made upon it. It has admitted this, but as long as it can get rate increases, why should it worry? It flaunts the CRTC's instructions to improve service and it has been doing so for years. I call upon the government, through
the Minister of Communications, to roll back the rate increases to B.C. Tel and I hope to hear that this is exactly what the government is going to do.
The B.C. Tel profit picture bears examination. At the very moment it announces this mammoth lay-off, it declares a dividend to its shareholders of approximately $13 million. Its total dividend payout for 1982 will be about $23.8 million, yet it claims that due to "economic conditions'' it must lay off workers and deprive consumers of service.
It is odd that in the July 26 issue of The Financial Post Jack Shriner is quoted as saying, at the Pemberton Securities seminar, that only four B.C. companies are in good health and one of these is B.C. Tel. Yet a rate increase of 15 per cent has just been granted to B.C. Tel and service will become even worse as it short-changes consumers and lays off workers to the tune of a saving in wages of approximately $30 million.
My second question in this regard was directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy), who should be concerned about the whole caper since it is an assault on the UIC as well as on the CRTC.
The other day in the House the minister said that both employers and employees contribute to UIC, so the federal government has no responsibility if it is being abused. What absolute nonsense. The government is always very concerned if an individual abuses the UIC. It is always checking individuals to see if they are abusing the UIC. But a private company can lay off 2,000 or more workers for up to six months and the government says it has no concern. Apparently this is not regarded as an abuse of UIC. The government's only concern is with abuses by individuals, not possible abuses by private companies.
Apparently in the minister's mind, what is good for B.C. Tel is good for Canada. 1 think it is time the minister woke up to the possibility that by the unnecessary lay-off of workers, private industry is not only depriving consumers of services but is actually abusing the unemployment insurance program.
I hope to have answers to these two questions tonight. Why have rate increases granted by the CRTC over the past two years not been substantially reduced, since B.C. Tel is constantly flouting the CRTC, and why has the Minister of Employment and Immigration not been concerned about the possible abuse caused by this deliberate and unnecessary layoff of employees at B.C. Tel?
There is a third question I have not yet raised and did not raise in the House. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary cannot reply to it tonight, but in case he has looked into the matter perhaps he could also tell the House whether or not in his view the Canada Labour Code has been circumvented with this minimal six-week notice of lay-off which B.C. Tel gave its employees. Is six weeks the correct length of time or should it not, under the Canada Labour Code, have been substantially longer than that?
July 5, 1982

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subtopic: CANADIAN RADIO-TELEVISION AND TELECOMMUNICATION COMMISSION-RATE INCREASES GRANTED TO BRITISH COLUMBIA TELEPHONE COMPANY. (B) EFFECT OF COMPANY LAY-OFFS ON UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question posed by the hon. member raises two issues: the relationship between the level of service quality and rate increases approved by the CRTC; second, B.C. Tel's recent announcement regarding the lay-off of some 2,200 employees.
As you may know, service quality has been a central issue in the last several rate case-proceedings. Since the CRTC took over the job of regulating the telephone companies, it has spent considerable time and effort to develop suitable service level objectives for all of the carriers it regulates. The commission has been very persistent in encouraging B.C. Tel to improve its performance where necessary to meet these new objectives.
In its decision 81-3 in January, 1981, the commission stated that the approved rates were "predicated upon the expectation that adequate service quality will be available to subscribers while those rates were in effect and that the minimum acceptable level of service quality will have been achieved by the fourth quarter of 1981."
In its next rate decision, 82-5, issued in May, 1982, the CRTC again addressed the issue of service quality. The commission noted that while certain service standards had improved, others had not been met. In considering what action to take regarding rate increases, the commission noted that the company suffered a considerable work stoppage as a result of a strike by the TWU and that this may have delayed some expected improvements. However, since the company has not attained the required level of service quality, the commission granted lower rate increases than would otherwise have been the case.
